# https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/langchain-tools/

## Companion files

CI-tested scripts that run this page's examples end to end. A script that exits 0 has passed its checks.

They need Unity Catalog 0.7.0 with MLflow, simulated S3, and PostgreSQL running. To start it (also `environment` in this file's frontmatter):

```bash
curl -fsSL https://unitycatalog.io/docs/env/uc-mlflow.tar.gz | tar -xz
cd uc-docs-env/uc-mlflow && docker compose up -d --wait
export AWS_ALLOW_HTTP=true
export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:9000
export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3=http://localhost:9000
export AWS_REGION=us-east-1
export MLFLOW_AI_GATEWAY_URL=http://localhost:8080/ai-gateway
export MLFLOW_ENABLE_PROXY_MULTIPART_DOWNLOAD=false
export MLFLOW_ENABLE_PROXY_MULTIPART_UPLOAD=false
export MLFLOW_REGISTRY_URI=uc:http://localhost:8080
export MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI=http://localhost:8080
export UNITY_CATALOG_URL=http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog
```

- [`error_py313.py`](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/langchain-tools/snippets/error_py313.py) (Python): On Python 3.13.0-3.13.2, an error a catalog function raises is lost through the tool.
  - run: `AWS_ALLOW_HTTP=true AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:9000 AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3=http://localhost:9000 AWS_REGION=us-east-1 MLFLOW_AI_GATEWAY_URL=http://localhost:8080/ai-gateway MLFLOW_ENABLE_PROXY_MULTIPART_DOWNLOAD=false MLFLOW_ENABLE_PROXY_MULTIPART_UPLOAD=false MLFLOW_REGISTRY_URI=uc:http://localhost:8080 MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI=http://localhost:8080 UNITY_CATALOG_URL=http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog uv run https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/langchain-tools/snippets/error_py313.py`
- [`tool_types.py`](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/langchain-tools/snippets/tool_types.py) (Python): Which parameter and return types survive each way an agent calls a tool.
  - run: `AWS_ALLOW_HTTP=true AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:9000 AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3=http://localhost:9000 AWS_REGION=us-east-1 MLFLOW_AI_GATEWAY_URL=http://localhost:8080/ai-gateway MLFLOW_ENABLE_PROXY_MULTIPART_DOWNLOAD=false MLFLOW_ENABLE_PROXY_MULTIPART_UPLOAD=false MLFLOW_REGISTRY_URI=uc:http://localhost:8080 MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI=http://localhost:8080 UNITY_CATALOG_URL=http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog uv run https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/langchain-tools/snippets/tool_types.py`
- [`tools.py`](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/langchain-tools/snippets/tools.py) (Python): Turn Unity Catalog functions into LangChain tools, inspect them, call them,
  - run: `AWS_ALLOW_HTTP=true AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:9000 AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3=http://localhost:9000 AWS_REGION=us-east-1 MLFLOW_AI_GATEWAY_URL=http://localhost:8080/ai-gateway MLFLOW_ENABLE_PROXY_MULTIPART_DOWNLOAD=false MLFLOW_ENABLE_PROXY_MULTIPART_UPLOAD=false MLFLOW_REGISTRY_URI=uc:http://localhost:8080 MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI=http://localhost:8080 UNITY_CATALOG_URL=http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog uv run tools.py`
  - save [`pricing.py`](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/langchain-tools/snippets/pricing.py) beside it first; the script imports it

Register Python functions in [Unity Catalog](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/what-is-unity-catalog/ "The open-source reference server implementing the Unity Catalog specification."), build LangChain tools from them with `UCFunctionToolkit` from the `unitycatalog-langchain` package, hand the tools to an agent, and trace its calls with MLflow. The catalog stores each function's signature, descriptions, and source code. The agent's machine runs the code, not the server. For where functions sit among the other catalog objects, see [Core concepts](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/uc-basics/).

> **Prerequisites**
>
> - [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-started/get-docker/) with Compose v2, for the local environment.
> - Unity Catalog 0.7.0 with MLflow, simulated S3, and PostgreSQL, running: [Run a local Unity Catalog server](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/run-local-server/).
> - [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/).
> - With authorization enabled, the privileges for each task: [Control who can call a function](#control-who-can-call-a-function).

## Set up the client

Start Python with the LangChain integration, LangGraph, MLflow, and the MLflow chat model for LangChain:

```bash
EXECUTOR_MAX_MEMORY_LIMIT=4096 uv run --python 3.12 --with unitycatalog-langchain==0.4.0 --with langgraph-prebuilt==1.0.8 --with mlflow==3.17.0 --with langchain-community==0.4.1 python -m asyncio
```

Use Python 3.12, or 3.13.3 or later. On 3.13.0 to 3.13.2, a function that raises loses its traceback: the tool returns the generic "no output was produced" notice under `error` instead.

The function sandbox caps each call's virtual memory at `EXECUTOR_MAX_MEMORY_LIMIT` megabytes (100 by default), a limit that applies only on Linux. The command sets it to 4096, the value this page's scripts run with.

Create the function client:

`tools.py`

```python
from unitycatalog.ai.core.client import (
    UnitycatalogClient,
    UnitycatalogFunctionClient,
)
from unitycatalog.client import ApiClient, CatalogsApi, Configuration

config = Configuration(host="http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog")
api = ApiClient(config)
client = UnitycatalogFunctionClient(api_client=api)
```

> **Tip**
>
> Always pass this client to the toolkit as `client=`. Without it, the toolkit uses the default client set with `set_uc_function_client`. If none is set, it [tries a Databricks client](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/blob/v0.7.0/ai/core/src/unitycatalog/ai/core/base.py) when Databricks Connect with serverless support is installed. Otherwise it raises `ValueError: No client provided, either set the client when creating a
> toolkit or set the default client using
> unitycatalog.ai.core.client.set_uc_function_client(client).`

## Register the functions the agent may call

The agent decides when to call a function from its description. The docstring's summary becomes the tool's description, and each `Args:` line becomes that argument's description.

Create a catalog and a schema for the functions:

`tools.py`

```python
uc = UnitycatalogClient(api_client=api)
await uc.create_catalog_async(name="tools", comment="Functions for apps and agents")
await uc.create_schema_async(name="pricing", catalog_name="tools")
```

Save two functions as `pricing.py`, in the folder where the session runs:

`pricing.py`

```python
def order_total(quantity: int, unit_price: float, discount_pct: float = 0.0) -> float:
    """
    Calculate the total price of an order line after a percentage discount.

    Args:
        quantity: Number of units ordered.
        unit_price: Price of one unit.
        discount_pct: Discount in percent, from 0 to 100.

    Returns:
        The discounted total, rounded to two decimals.
    """
    return round(quantity * unit_price * (1 - discount_pct / 100), 2)


```

`pricing.py`

```python
def shipping_cost(weight_kg: float, express: bool) -> float:
    """
    Calculate the shipping cost of a parcel.

    Args:
        weight_kg: Weight of the parcel in kilograms, greater than zero.
        express: Whether to ship with next-day delivery.

    Returns:
        The shipping cost, rounded to two decimals.
    """
    if weight_kg <= 0:
        raise ValueError("weight_kg must be greater than zero")
    rate = 4.5 if express else 2.0
    return round(5.0 + rate * weight_kg, 2)


```

Then register them:

`tools.py`

```python
from pricing import order_total, shipping_cost

for func in (order_total, shipping_cost):
    await client.create_python_function_async(
        func=func, catalog="tools", schema="pricing"
    )
```

> **Note**
>
> A model sends its arguments as JSON. On the agent path this page uses (see [Give the tools to an agent](#give-the-tools-to-an-agent)), each parameter type reaches the function like this:
>
> | Type                                 | What the function gets                                                                                                                           |
> | ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
> | `STRING`, `INT`, `BIGINT`, `BOOLEAN` | The value.                                                                                                                                       |
> | `DOUBLE`                             | The value. An integer is converted.                                                                                                              |
> | `DECIMAL`                            | A `Decimal` when the model sends a string such as `"1.25"`. A JSON number fails.                                                                 |
> | `TIMESTAMP`                          | The string the model sent, not a `datetime`.                                                                                                     |
> | `BINARY`                             | The bytes of the text, without base64 decoding.                                                                                                  |
> | `DATE`, `INTERVAL`, `STRUCT`         | Nothing: the call fails with `ValueError: Parameter <name> should be of type ColumnTypeName.DATE …` (or the type in question).                   |
> | `ARRAY`, `MAP`                       | The value on the first call. Every later call on the same client returns `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'` (or `'dict'`) as the tool's error. |
>
> A `BOOLEAN` parameter with a default registers the default as text, `"False"` or `"True"`, so a tool call that leaves the argument out fails: the tool passes the text default to the client's type check. Give `BOOLEAN` parameters no default.
>
> Return values of type `ARRAY`, `MAP`, `STRUCT`, `BOOLEAN`, and `DOUBLE` work. For a `DATE`, `TIMESTAMP`, `DECIMAL`, or `BINARY` return value, the tool call raises `TypeError: Object of type date is not JSON serializable` (or `datetime`, `Decimal`, `bytes`).

## Choose which functions become tools

List the functions by full name to build the toolkit:

`tools.py`

```python
from unitycatalog.ai.langchain.toolkit import UCFunctionToolkit

toolkit = UCFunctionToolkit(
    function_names=[
        "tools.pricing.order_total",
        "tools.pricing.shipping_cost",
    ],
    client=client,
)
tools = toolkit.tools
```

Each tool's name is the function's full name with `__` in place of the dots:

`tools.py`

```python
print([tool.name for tool in tools])
# ['tools__pricing__order_total', 'tools__pricing__shipping_cost']
```

A name longer than 64 characters is [cut to its last 64](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/blob/v0.7.0/ai/core/src/unitycatalog/ai/core/utils/function_processing_utils.py).

To include every function in a schema, use `catalog.schema.*`:

`tools.py`

```python
toolkit = UCFunctionToolkit(function_names=["tools.pricing.*"], client=client)
```

> **Warning**
>
> A wildcard also picks up functions that someone registers in the schema later: the next toolkit you build from it gives the agent those functions too. List the functions by name to keep an explicit allowlist of what the agent may call.

## Check what the model sees

Print a tool's description and its arguments:

`tools.py`

```python
order_tool = tools[0]
print(order_tool.description)
print(order_tool.args)
```

The description is the docstring's summary, `Calculate the total price of an
order line after a percentage discount.` Each argument has a JSON Schema type (`integer` for `quantity`, `number` for `unit_price`) and the description from its `Args:` line. A default is added to the description, as in `Discount in
percent, from 0 to 100. (Default: 0.0)`.

## Call a tool directly

Call a tool before you hand it to an agent, to check the function and its arguments. A call returns a JSON string:

`tools.py`

```python
output = order_tool.invoke(
    {"quantity": 3, "unit_price": 19.99, "discount_pct": 10.0}
)
print(output)  # {"format": "SCALAR", "value": 53.97}
print(json.loads(output)["value"])  # 53.97
```

The tool's schema converts an integer for a `DOUBLE` parameter, so the tool accepts `20` for `unit_price`, which a direct client call rejects. A direct `invoke` also turns every argument into JSON text (`default=str`) before the client checks its type. So `DATE`, `DECIMAL`, `BINARY`, `INTERVAL`, and `STRUCT` arguments fail here, even the ones the agent path accepts.

When the function raises, the call doesn't. It returns the traceback under `error`, which is what the agent sees:

`tools.py`

```python
shipping_tool = tools[1]
output = shipping_tool.invoke({"weight_kg": -1.0, "express": False})
print(json.loads(output)["error"])
# Traceback (most recent call last): ... ValueError: weight_kg must be greater than zero
```

Arguments the schema can't accept raise pydantic's `ValidationError` before the function runs. So do arguments the function doesn't declare (`Extra inputs are
not permitted`):

`tools.py`

```python
from pydantic import ValidationError

try:
    order_tool.invoke({"quantity": "three", "unit_price": 19.99})
except ValidationError as exc:
    print(exc)  # quantity: Input should be a valid integer ...
```

A function that returns a falsy value, such as `0`, `False`, `""`, `None`, `[]`, or `{}`, returns a notice instead of the value:

`tools.py`

```python
output = order_tool.invoke({"quantity": 0, "unit_price": 19.99})
print(json.loads(output)["value"])
# The function execution has completed, but no output was produced. ...
```

When the model needs to see a zero or an empty result, return a value that isn't falsy, such as a string or a non-empty map.

## Give the tools to an agent

LangChain's `create_agent` accepts the tools, but with the Unity Catalog function client they need an async adapter first.

### Workaround: run the tools on the session's event loop

As built, `toolkit.tools` fail inside an agent. Running the agent with `invoke` fails with `RuntimeError: … attached to a different loop`, and with `ainvoke` it fails with `RuntimeError: Timeout context manager should be used inside a
task`. LangGraph runs the tools' synchronous functions in worker threads, and the client's connection belongs to the session's event loop.

As a workaround, give each tool an asynchronous function that calls the client on the session's loop:

`tools.py`

```python
def run_on_this_loop(tool):
    async def run(**arguments):
        result = await client.execute_function_async(
            tool.uc_function_name, parameters=arguments
        )
        return result.to_json()

    tool.coroutine = run
    return tool

agent_tools = [run_on_this_loop(tool) for tool in tools]
```

### Run the agent

The agent needs a chat model in `model`. Set it first: point it at a gateway endpoint as in [Route the model through the MLflow AI Gateway](#route-the-model-through-the-mlflow-ai-gateway), or assign any LangChain chat model that supports tool calling. Then create the agent with the adapted tools and ask it a question:

`tools.py`

```python
from langchain.agents import create_agent

agent = create_agent(model, tools=agent_tools)
result = await agent.ainvoke(
    {
        "messages": [
            {
                "role": "user",
                "content": "Price 3 units at 19.99 with 10% off, shipped express at 2 kg.",
            }
        ]
    }
)
for message in result["messages"]:
    print(message.type, message.content)
```

The messages are your question, each tool call the model made, a `tool` message with each function's JSON result, and the model's answer.

## Trace the agent's tool calls with MLflow

MLflow's LangChain autologging records each agent run as a trace and sends it to the environment's MLflow tracking server, in the `langchain-tools` experiment. The `MLFLOW_ENABLE_PROXY_MULTIPART_*` settings keep trace data going through the tracking server, whose download links name an address only the environment can reach. Turn it on, then run the agent again:

`tools.py`

```python
import os

import mlflow

os.environ["MLFLOW_ENABLE_PROXY_MULTIPART_DOWNLOAD"] = "false"
os.environ["MLFLOW_ENABLE_PROXY_MULTIPART_UPLOAD"] = "false"
mlflow.set_tracking_uri("http://localhost:8080")
mlflow.set_experiment("langchain-tools")
mlflow.langchain.autolog()
```

MLflow writes traces in the background, so flush them before you read them back. Print the spans of the latest trace:

`tools.py`

```python
mlflow.flush_trace_async_logging()
trace = mlflow.search_traces(max_results=1, return_type="list")[0]
for span in trace.data.spans:
    print(span.span_type, span.name)
# CHAIN LangGraph
# CHAIN model
# CHAT_MODEL ...
# CHAIN tools
# TOOL tools__pricing__order_total
# ...
```

The trace has one span for the agent's graph, one for each model turn, and one `TOOL` span for each function call. A tool span records the arguments the model sent and the tool message it got back. To browse the same traces, open the `langchain-tools` experiment in the MLflow UI at <http://localhost:8080/mlflow/>.

## Route the model through the MLflow AI Gateway

The MLflow AI Gateway holds the provider key, so the agent's process needs only the gateway's URL and an endpoint name.

> **Warning**
>
> This section needs a real provider key, so CI doesn't test it. These steps were checked locally against a fake OpenAI-compatible server standing in for the provider.

Save the endpoint as `gateway.yaml`, with your provider, model, and base URL:

`gateway.yaml`

```yaml
endpoints:
  - name: chat
    endpoint_type: llm/v1/chat
    model:
      provider: openai
      name: gpt-4o-mini
      config:
        # The gateway reads the key from this environment variable.
        openai_api_key: $OPENAI_API_KEY
        # Any OpenAI-compatible server works here, including a local one.
        openai_api_base: https://api.openai.com/v1
```

In the same folder, with your provider's key in `OPENAI_API_KEY`, start the gateway:

`start_gateway.sh`

```bash
uv run --python 3.12 --with "mlflow[gateway]==3.17.0" \
  mlflow gateway start --config-path gateway.yaml --port 5050
```

In the Python session, point `model` at the gateway's `chat` endpoint, then run the agent:

`gateway_agent.py`

```python
from langchain_community.chat_models import ChatMlflow

model = ChatMlflow(target_uri="http://localhost:5050", endpoint="chat")
```

## Control who can call a function

The toolkit fetches each function from the server when you build a tool, and the client fetches it again on every call ([toolkit](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/blob/v0.7.0/ai/integrations/langchain/src/unitycatalog/ai/langchain/toolkit.py), [client](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/blob/v0.7.0/ai/core/src/unitycatalog/ai/core/client.py)). With authorization enabled, the server returns a function to a caller who ([`FunctionService.java`](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/blob/v0.7.0/server/src/main/java/io/unitycatalog/server/service/FunctionService.java)):

- owns the metastore or the function's catalog,
- owns the function's schema and has `USE CATALOG` on its catalog, or
- has `USE CATALOG` on the catalog, `USE SCHEMA` on the schema, and `EXECUTE` on the function or owns it.

Registering a function needs `USE CATALOG` on the catalog (or its ownership), plus `USE SCHEMA` and `CREATE FUNCTION` on the schema (or its ownership). Creating the catalog needs `CREATE CATALOG` on the metastore (or its ownership), and creating the schema needs `USE CATALOG` and `CREATE SCHEMA` on the catalog (or its ownership). For how these grants inherit, see [Core concepts](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/uc-basics/).

The function then runs on the agent's machine. By default the client runs it in a sandboxed subprocess, which restricts imports and file access and caps CPU time and memory. It runs inside the agent's own process only if you create the client with `execution_mode="local"`.

> **Note**
>
> These rules come from the server's source. These docs haven't run them against a server with authorization enabled.

## Next steps

- Register, inspect, and run functions step by step in [Working with Python functions](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/tutorials/first-python-function/).
- Learn how functions, schemas, and the `EXECUTE` privilege fit together in [Core concepts](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/uc-basics/).

---

# https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/manage-models/

## Companion files

CI-tested scripts that run this page's examples end to end. A script that exits 0 has passed its checks.

They need Unity Catalog 0.7.0 with MLflow, simulated S3, and PostgreSQL running. To start it (also `environment` in this file's frontmatter):

```bash
curl -fsSL https://unitycatalog.io/docs/env/uc-mlflow.tar.gz | tar -xz
cd uc-docs-env/uc-mlflow && docker compose up -d --wait
export AWS_ALLOW_HTTP=true
export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:9000
export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3=http://localhost:9000
export AWS_REGION=us-east-1
export MLFLOW_AI_GATEWAY_URL=http://localhost:8080/ai-gateway
export MLFLOW_ENABLE_PROXY_MULTIPART_DOWNLOAD=false
export MLFLOW_ENABLE_PROXY_MULTIPART_UPLOAD=false
export MLFLOW_REGISTRY_URI=uc:http://localhost:8080
export MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI=http://localhost:8080
export UNITY_CATALOG_URL=http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog
```

- [`models.sh`](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/manage-models/snippets/models.sh) (Shell): View, update, rename, and delete registered models with the uc CLI.
  - run: `bash models.sh` from `uc-docs-env/uc-mlflow`
- [`models_mlflow.py`](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/manage-models/snippets/models_mlflow.py) (Python): Register, view, load, update, and delete Unity Catalog models with MLflow.
  - run: `AWS_ALLOW_HTTP=true AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:9000 AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3=http://localhost:9000 AWS_REGION=us-east-1 MLFLOW_AI_GATEWAY_URL=http://localhost:8080/ai-gateway MLFLOW_ENABLE_PROXY_MULTIPART_DOWNLOAD=false MLFLOW_ENABLE_PROXY_MULTIPART_UPLOAD=false MLFLOW_REGISTRY_URI=uc:http://localhost:8080 MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI=http://localhost:8080 UNITY_CATALOG_URL=http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog uv run https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/manage-models/snippets/models_mlflow.py`
- [`models_sdk.py`](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/manage-models/snippets/models_sdk.py) (Python): View, update, rename, and delete registered models with the Python SDK.
  - run: `AWS_ALLOW_HTTP=true AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:9000 AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3=http://localhost:9000 AWS_REGION=us-east-1 MLFLOW_AI_GATEWAY_URL=http://localhost:8080/ai-gateway MLFLOW_ENABLE_PROXY_MULTIPART_DOWNLOAD=false MLFLOW_ENABLE_PROXY_MULTIPART_UPLOAD=false MLFLOW_REGISTRY_URI=uc:http://localhost:8080 MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI=http://localhost:8080 UNITY_CATALOG_URL=http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog uv run https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/manage-models/snippets/models_sdk.py`

A [registered model](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/models-and-mlflow/ "A governed ML model.") in [Unity Catalog](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/what-is-unity-catalog/ "The open-source reference server implementing the Unity Catalog specification.") lives in a schema and has a three-level name, such as `unity.manage_models.linear`. It holds numbered versions, and each version has its own copy of the model's files in the catalog's managed storage. MLflow's tracking server keeps the runs and the logged models. Unity Catalog keeps the registered models and their versions ([how the two services divide the work](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/models-and-mlflow/)).

On this page, MLflow uploads a version's files and loads them. MLflow, the Python SDK, and the CLI all view, update, and delete models and versions, and only the SDK and the CLI rename them.

Each task lists the privileges that the server's [authorization rules for models](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/blob/v0.7.0/server/src/main/java/io/unitycatalog/server/service/ModelService.java) require when authorization is enabled.

> **Prerequisites**
>
> - [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-started/get-docker/) with Compose v2, for the local environment.
> - Unity Catalog 0.7.0 with MLflow, simulated S3, and PostgreSQL, running: [Run a local Unity Catalog server](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/run-local-server/).
> - [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/).
> - A catalog with managed storage, such as `unity`, and a schema in it, such as `unity.manage_models`: [Manage catalogs and schemas](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/manage-catalogs-and-schemas/).
> - For the Python SDK and CLI examples, the model `unity.manage_models.linear` with versions 1 and 2, registered with MLflow as in [Register a model version](#register-a-model-version).

## Set up the client

Set up the client for your interface:

**MLflow**

Start Python with MLflow, boto3 for the version's files in S3, and scikit-learn, the library the example model uses:

```bash
uv run --python 3.12 --with mlflow==3.17.0 --with boto3==1.43.114 --with scikit-learn==1.9.1 python
```

Point MLflow at the tracking server and at Unity Catalog's registry. The `uc:` prefix on the registry URI selects MLflow's Unity Catalog registry, and `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3` points MLflow at the environment's S3-compatible store. The `MLFLOW_ENABLE_PROXY_MULTIPART_*` settings keep the logged model's files going through the tracking server, whose download links name an address only the environment can reach:

`models_mlflow.py`

```python
import os

import mlflow
from mlflow import MlflowClient

os.environ["AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3"] = "http://localhost:9000"
os.environ["MLFLOW_ENABLE_PROXY_MULTIPART_DOWNLOAD"] = "false"
os.environ["MLFLOW_ENABLE_PROXY_MULTIPART_UPLOAD"] = "false"
mlflow.set_tracking_uri("http://localhost:8080")
mlflow.set_registry_uri("uc:http://localhost:8080")
client = MlflowClient()
```

**Python SDK**

Start Python with the SDK:

```bash
uv run --with unitycatalog-client==0.7.0 python -m asyncio
```

`models_sdk.py`

```python
from unitycatalog.client import (
    ApiClient,
    Configuration,
    ModelVersionsApi,
    RegisteredModelsApi,
    UpdateModelVersion,
    UpdateRegisteredModel,
)

api = ApiClient(Configuration(host="http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog"))
models = RegisteredModelsApi(api)
versions = ModelVersionsApi(api)
```

**CLI**

`models.sh`

```bash
uc() { docker exec unitycatalog bin/uc "$@"; }
```

The examples use one model, `unity.manage_models.linear`. The next section registers it with versions 1 and 2, and every section after it starts from there.

## Register a model version

Registering needs a model logged in MLflow. To follow along, train two small linear models, y = 2x + 1 and y = 3x + 1, and log each in its own run:

`models_mlflow.py`

```python
import pandas as pd
from mlflow.models import infer_signature
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

X = pd.DataFrame({"x": [0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]})
mlflow.set_experiment("manage-models")
model_uris = []
for slope in (2, 3):
    fitted = LinearRegression().fit(X, slope * X["x"] + 1)
    with mlflow.start_run():
        info = mlflow.sklearn.log_model(
            fitted,
            name="linear",
            signature=infer_signature(X, fitted.predict(X)),
            pip_requirements=["mlflow==3.17.0", "scikit-learn==1.9.1"],
        )
    model_uris.append(info.model_uri)

print(model_uris)
```

The session prints the two logged models' URIs, each of the form `models:/m-<id>`.

Register the first one under the model's name. If the model doesn't exist, MLflow creates it with version 1:

`models_mlflow.py`

```python
version = mlflow.register_model(model_uris[0], "unity.manage_models.linear")
print(version.version, version.status)
```

MLflow reports:

```text
Successfully registered model 'unity.manage_models.linear'.
Created version '1' of model 'unity.manage_models.linear'.
1 READY
```

Register the second one under the same name. MLflow adds the next version:

`models_mlflow.py`

```python
version = mlflow.register_model(model_uris[1], "unity.manage_models.linear")
print(version.version, version.status)
```

```text
Registered model 'unity.manage_models.linear' already exists. Creating a new version of this model...
Created version '2' of model 'unity.manage_models.linear'.
2 READY
```

Both calls also print a line about waiting for the version and progress bars. One call creates the version, copies the logged model's files into the catalog's managed storage, and marks the version `READY`. MLflow writes the files with temporary credentials that Unity Catalog issues for that one version. See [Credential vending](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/credential-vending/).

> **Note**
>
> Version numbers aren't reused. If you delete version 2, the next registration creates version 3.

MLflow doesn't pass `tags` to Unity Catalog. Tags given to `register_model` or `create_registered_model` are dropped without an error.

**Required privileges:** `mlflow.register_model` [tries to create the model first](https://github.com/mlflow/mlflow/blob/v3.17.0/mlflow/tracking/_model_registry/fluent.py#L177-L188) and continues only if it already exists, so every call needs all of these:

- To create the model, even when it exists: `USE_CATALOG` or ownership on the catalog, and on the schema either ownership, or `USE_SCHEMA` plus `CREATE_MODEL` (or `CREATE_FUNCTION`). Whoever creates the model owns it.
- To add and finalize the version: ownership of the catalog; or `USE_CATALOG` and ownership of the schema; or `USE_CATALOG`, `USE_SCHEMA`, and ownership of the model.
- To [write the version's files](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/blob/v0.7.0/server/src/main/java/io/unitycatalog/server/service/TemporaryModelVersionCredentialsService.java#L40-L47): ownership of the model, plus `USE_SCHEMA` or ownership on the schema and `USE_CATALOG` or ownership on the catalog. Owning the catalog doesn't replace owning the model.

## View models and versions

**MLflow**

`models_mlflow.py`

```python
for model in client.search_registered_models():
    print(model.name, model.description)

for v in client.search_model_versions("name='unity.manage_models.linear'"):
    print(v.version, v.status, v.source)

```

Search takes no `filter_string` or `order_by` for models, and no `order_by` for versions. Either one raises `Argument '…' is unsupported for models in the Unity Catalog.`

**Python SDK**

`models_sdk.py`

```python
listed = await models.list_registered_models(
    catalog_name="unity", schema_name="manage_models"
)
for model in listed.registered_models:
    print(model.full_name, model.storage_location)

listed = await versions.list_model_versions(
    full_name="unity.manage_models.linear"
)
for v in listed.model_versions:
    print(v.version, v.status.value, v.source)

v = await versions.get_model_version(
    full_name="unity.manage_models.linear", version=1
)
print(v.status.value, v.storage_location)
```

**CLI**

`models.sh`

```bash
uc registered_model list --catalog unity --schema manage_models --output jsonPretty
uc model_version list --full_name unity.manage_models.linear --output jsonPretty
uc model_version get --full_name unity.manage_models.linear --version 1 --output jsonPretty
```

A version's `status` is `READY` once registration finishes. Its `source` is the logged model it was copied from, `models:/m-<id>`. Its `run_id` is set only when you register from a `runs:/<run-id>/<path>` URI. A model's `storage_location` is a directory in the catalog's managed storage, and each version's files sit below it, under `versions/`.

**Required privileges:** one of ownership of the metastore; ownership of the catalog; `USE_CATALOG` and ownership of the schema; or `EXECUTE` or ownership on the model, plus `USE_SCHEMA` and `USE_CATALOG`. A list of models returns only the models you could get.

## Load a model version

Load a version by its number, and get the location of its files:

`models_mlflow.py`

```python
model = mlflow.pyfunc.load_model("models:/unity.manage_models.linear/1")
print(model.metadata.signature)
print(model.predict(pd.DataFrame({"x": [10.0]})))
print(client.get_model_version_download_uri("unity.manage_models.linear", "1"))
```

The session prints the version's signature, with the input column `x` as a `double`, then the prediction `[21.]`, since version 1 fits y = 2x + 1. The signature comes from the version's files, not from Unity Catalog's record of the version. The location has the form `s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/unity/__unitystorage/catalogs/<id>/models/<id>/versions/<id>`. MLflow reads the files with read-only credentials from Unity Catalog.

Load by number only. Unity Catalog's registry has no aliases and no stages, so `models:/<name>@<alias>` and `models:/<name>/latest` raise `NotImplementedError: Method not implemented`. So do setting an alias, `get_latest_versions`, and `transition_model_version_stage`.

**Required privileges:** the privileges to view the version, and to [read its files](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/blob/v0.7.0/server/src/main/java/io/unitycatalog/server/service/TemporaryModelVersionCredentialsService.java#L40-L47), `EXECUTE` or ownership on the model, plus `USE_SCHEMA` or ownership on the schema and `USE_CATALOG` or ownership on the catalog. Owning the catalog or the metastore doesn't replace these.

## Update comments

Besides the model's name, a comment is the only metadata you can change on a model or a version. Set one on the model and one on version 2:

**MLflow**

MLflow calls the comment `description`:

`models_mlflow.py`

```python
client.update_registered_model(
    "unity.manage_models.linear",
    description="Predicts y from x with a linear fit",
)
client.update_model_version(
    "unity.manage_models.linear", "2", description="Retrained on the new slope"
)
```

**Python SDK**

`models_sdk.py`

```python
await models.update_registered_model(
    full_name="unity.manage_models.linear",
    update_registered_model=UpdateRegisteredModel(
        comment="Predicts y from x with a linear fit"
    ),
)
await versions.update_model_version(
    full_name="unity.manage_models.linear",
    version=2,
    update_model_version=UpdateModelVersion(
        comment="Retrained on the new slope"
    ),
)
```

**CLI**

`models.sh`

```bash
uc registered_model update --full_name unity.manage_models.linear \
  --comment "Predicts y from x with a linear fit"
uc model_version update --full_name unity.manage_models.linear --version 2 \
  --comment "Retrained on the new slope"
```

The Python sessions echo the updated model and version. Other versions keep their comments. Models and versions have no tags: `set_registered_model_tag` and `set_model_version_tag` raise `NotImplementedError`. A version's signature and input example live in its files, not in Unity Catalog.

**Required privileges:** one of ownership of the catalog; `USE_CATALOG` and ownership of the schema; or `USE_CATALOG`, `USE_SCHEMA`, and ownership of the model. The same holds for a model's comment and a version's.

## Rename a model

Rename a model with the Python SDK or the CLI. `new_name` is the model's name within its schema. MLflow's `rename_registered_model` raises `NotImplementedError`.

The example renames the model to `linear_regression` and prints the result, then renames it back, so the examples below still find it as `linear`:

**Python SDK**

`models_sdk.py`

```python
renamed = await models.update_registered_model(
    full_name="unity.manage_models.linear",
    update_registered_model=UpdateRegisteredModel(new_name="linear_regression"),
)
print(renamed.full_name)

# Rename it back, so the steps below find it by its first name.
await models.update_registered_model(
    full_name="unity.manage_models.linear_regression",
    update_registered_model=UpdateRegisteredModel(new_name="linear"),
)
```

**CLI**

`models.sh`

```bash
uc registered_model update --full_name unity.manage_models.linear \
  --new_name linear_regression --output jsonPretty
# Rename it back, so the steps below find it by its first name.
uc registered_model update --full_name unity.manage_models.linear_regression \
  --new_name linear
```

The model keeps its id, storage location, comment, and versions. Only its name changes.

**Required privileges:** the same as for updating a comment.

## Delete versions and models

**Required privileges:** to delete a version, or a model with or without `force`, the same as for updating a comment.

### Delete a version

**MLflow**

`models_mlflow.py`

```python
client.delete_model_version("unity.manage_models.linear", "2")
```

**Python SDK**

`models_sdk.py`

```python
await versions.delete_model_version(
    full_name="unity.manage_models.linear", version=2
)
```

**CLI**

`models.sh`

```bash
uc model_version delete --full_name unity.manage_models.linear --version 2
```

### Delete a model

A model that still has versions is deleted only with `force`. Without it, the server refuses with `Unable to delete a registered model with existing model versions`. The Python SDK and the CLI pass `force`. MLflow can't, so its example deletes the versions first, a page of search results at a time, until none are left:

**MLflow**

`models_mlflow.py`

```python
name = "unity.manage_models.linear"
while versions := client.search_model_versions(f"name='{name}'"):
    for v in versions:
        client.delete_model_version(name, v.version)

client.delete_registered_model(name)
```

**Python SDK**

`models_sdk.py`

```python
await models.delete_registered_model(
    full_name="unity.manage_models.linear", force=True
)
```

When you're done, close the client:

`models_sdk.py`

```python
await api.close()
```

**CLI**

`models.sh`

```bash
uc registered_model delete --full_name unity.manage_models.linear --force true
```

### What happens to the files

The catalog entry goes at once. A background worker in the server deletes the version's or the model's directory in managed storage no sooner than [`server.storage-cleanup.initial-delay`](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/blob/v0.7.0/etc/conf/server.properties#L67-L76) after the delete, 7 days by default, and retries a deletion that fails. The run and the logged model on the MLflow tracking server, with their files, stay.

> **Warning**
>
> The delay isn't a recovery window: a deleted model or version can't be restored, and once the worker runs its files are gone for good. Load or copy anything you still need first.

## Next steps

- [Register and reload a model with MLflow](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/tutorials/register-model-mlflow/) to walk through logging and registering a model from the start.
- [Learn how credential vending works](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/credential-vending/), the mechanism that lets MLflow read and write a version's files.
- [Learn the core concepts](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/uc-basics/) to see where registered models sit in the namespace.

# https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/configure-spark/

## Companion files

CI-tested scripts that run this page's examples end to end. A script that exits 0 has passed its checks.

They need Unity Catalog 0.7.0 running. To start it (also `environment` in this file's frontmatter):

```bash
curl -fsSL https://unitycatalog.io/docs/env/unitycatalog.tar.gz | tar -xz
cd uc-docs-env/unitycatalog && docker compose up -d --wait
export UNITY_CATALOG_URL=http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog
```

- [`spark_session.py`](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/configure-spark/snippets/spark_session.py) (Python): Connect Spark to Unity Catalog and list what the catalog holds.
  - run: `UNITY_CATALOG_URL=http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog uv run https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/configure-spark/snippets/spark_session.py`

Apache Spark connects to a [Unity Catalog](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/what-is-unity-catalog/ "The open-source reference server implementing the Unity Catalog specification.") server through the Unity Catalog Spark connector, so that Spark SQL can name `catalog.schema.table` and read and write the tables it holds. The connector registers one Unity Catalog catalog as a Spark catalog. Delta Spark handles the table format, and from Delta 4.3.0 it reads and commits catalog-managed tables through the server's Delta API.

> **Prerequisites**
>
> - [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-started/get-docker/) with Compose v2, for the local environment.
> - Unity Catalog 0.7.0, running: [Run a local Unity Catalog server](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/run-local-server/).
> - [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/).
> - [Java 17](https://adoptium.net/temurin/releases/?version=17).

## Choose matching versions

The connector is built per Spark minor version. Its artifact name carries the Spark version, and it needs a Delta Spark build for the same Spark version:

| Spark                                                                                                                       | Unity Catalog connector                             | Delta Spark                           |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| 4.1 (tested here: PySpark 4.1.0)                                                                                            | `io.unitycatalog:unitycatalog-spark_4.1_2.13:0.7.0` | `io.delta:delta-spark_4.1_2.13:4.3.1` |
| 4.0                                                                                                                         | `io.unitycatalog:unitycatalog-spark_4.0_2.13:0.7.0` | `io.delta:delta-spark_4.0_2.13:4.3.1` |
| 4.2 (tested here: PySpark 4.2.0, in [Working with metric views](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/tutorials/first-metric-view/)) | `io.unitycatalog:unitycatalog-spark_4.2_2.13:0.7.0` | `io.delta:delta-spark_4.2_2.13:4.4.1` |

With a Delta Spark release older than 4.3.0, the connector quietly skips the Delta API, and catalog-managed tables don't work.

### Connector versions by release

Each Unity Catalog release publishes one connector artifact per Spark minor version, named `unitycatalog-spark_<spark>_2.13`. All of them are built for Scala 2.13. The release notes name a Delta Spark release that the connector works with. The connector's own tests build against the version in the last column, so where the two differ, the release notes name the newer release.

| Unity Catalog                                                             | Spark 4.0 | Spark 4.1 | Spark 4.2 | Delta Spark in the release notes | Delta Spark the connector tests with |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------- | --------- | --------- | -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| [0.7.0](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/releases/tag/v0.7.0) | ✓         | ✓         | ✓         | Not named                        | 4.3.1                                |
| [0.6.0](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/releases/tag/v0.6.0) | ✓         | ✓         | ✓         | 4.4.0                            | 4.3.1                                |
| [0.5.1](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/releases/tag/v0.5.1) | ✓         | ✓         | —         | Not named                        | 4.2.0                                |
| [0.5.0](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/releases/tag/v0.5.0) | ✓         | ✓         | —         | 4.3.0                            | 4.2.0                                |

Releases before 0.5.0 shipped a single `unitycatalog-spark_2.13` artifact.

## Configure the session

Register the catalog under a Spark catalog name and point it at the server. The Spark name is your choice. Using the Unity Catalog catalog's own name, here `unity`, keeps three-part names the same in Spark and in the catalog:

`spark_session.py`

```python
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

UC_SPARK = "io.unitycatalog:unitycatalog-spark_4.1_2.13:0.7.0"
DELTA_SPARK = "io.delta:delta-spark_4.1_2.13:4.3.1"

spark = (
    SparkSession.builder.appName("uc-spark")
    .config("spark.jars.packages", f"{UC_SPARK},{DELTA_SPARK}")
    .config("spark.sql.extensions", "io.delta.sql.DeltaSparkSessionExtension")
    .config(
        "spark.sql.catalog.spark_catalog",
        "org.apache.spark.sql.delta.catalog.DeltaCatalog",
    )
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.unity", "io.unitycatalog.spark.UCSingleCatalog")
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.unity.uri", "http://localhost:8080")
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.unity.auth.type", "static")
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.unity.auth.token", "not-used")
    .config("spark.sql.defaultCatalog", "unity")
    .getOrCreate()
)
```

Each setting has a job:

| Setting                                                   | Purpose                                                                                              |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `spark.jars.packages`                                     | Downloads the connector and Delta Spark.                                                             |
| `spark.sql.extensions`, `spark.sql.catalog.spark_catalog` | Enable Delta's SQL support in the session.                                                           |
| `spark.sql.catalog.<name>`                                | Registers the Unity Catalog catalog `<name>` with Spark. Repeat this block for each catalog you use. |
| `spark.sql.catalog.<name>.uri`                            | The server's base URL, without `/api/2.1/unity-catalog`.                                             |
| `spark.sql.catalog.<name>.auth.*`                         | How Spark authenticates. See the next section.                                                       |
| `spark.sql.defaultCatalog`                                | Lets queries leave out the catalog name.                                                             |

The same keys work as `--conf` options for `spark-submit`, `spark-sql`, and `pyspark`, with `--packages` in place of `spark.jars.packages`.

> **Tip**
>
> If you reach Maven through a mirror, add `.config("spark.jars.repositories", "https://<your-mirror>")` to the builder.

## Authenticate to the server

The connector always needs an authentication type, even when the server has authorization disabled. Without one, the first query fails with `Required configuration key 'type' is missing or empty`.

- **Static token.** Set `auth.type` to `static` and `auth.token` to a Unity Catalog access token. The local server above accepts any value. Older configurations set `token` instead, which still works. Set only one of the two.
- **OAuth client credentials.** Set `auth.type` to `oauth`, plus `auth.oauth.uri`, `auth.oauth.clientId`, and `auth.oauth.clientSecret`. `auth.oauth.scope` defaults to `all-apis`. The connector fetches and renews the token itself. This page doesn't test the OAuth flow.

Keep secrets out of source code. Read the token or client secret from the environment or a secret store when you build the session.

## Check the connection

List the catalog's schemas and the tables in one of them:

`spark_session.py`

```python
spark.sql("SHOW SCHEMAS").show()
spark.sql("SHOW TABLES IN default").show()
```

The sample catalog's `default` schema lists tables such as `numbers` and `marksheet`. These sample tables live inside the server's container, so this local Spark can list them but can't read their files. Create your own tables under a storage root that both sides can reach, as in [Create and update a catalog-managed Delta table](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/tutorials/managed-delta-table/).

## Tune storage credentials

When Spark reads or writes a table, the connector asks the server for short-lived storage credentials for that table's location. It applies them per table. Three catalog options control this, and the defaults suit most setups:

| Option                    | Default | Effect                                                                                                      |
| ------------------------- | ------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `renewCredential.enabled` | `true`  | Fetches new credentials before vended ones expire, so long jobs keep running.                               |
| `credScopedFs.enabled`    | `true`  | Caches file-system clients per credential, not per bucket, so tables in the same bucket don't share access. |
| `deltaRestApi.enabled`    | `true`  | Uses the Delta API for Delta tables. Catalog-managed tables need it.                                        |

Set them like the others, for example `spark.sql.catalog.unity.renewCredential.enabled`. For how the server decides what each credential may access, see [Credential vending](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/credential-vending/).

Option names and defaults come from the connector source, [`OptionsUtil.java`](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/blob/v0.7.0/connectors/spark/src/main/java/io/unitycatalog/spark/utils/OptionsUtil.java) and [`AuthConfigs.java`](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/blob/v0.7.0/clients/java/src/main/java/io/unitycatalog/client/auth/AuthConfigs.java).

## Next steps

- [Create and update a catalog-managed Delta table](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/tutorials/managed-delta-table/) puts this session to work.
- [Use DuckDB with Unity Catalog](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/duckdb/) and [Query Unity Catalog tables from Python DataFrame libraries](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/python-dataframes/) cover other engines.

---

# https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/duckdb/

## Companion files

CI-tested scripts that run this page's examples end to end. A script that exits 0 has passed its checks.

They need Unity Catalog 0.7.0 running. To start it (also `environment` in this file's frontmatter):

```bash
curl -fsSL https://unitycatalog.io/docs/env/unitycatalog.tar.gz | tar -xz
cd uc-docs-env/unitycatalog && docker compose up -d --wait
export UNITY_CATALOG_URL=http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog
```

- [`duckdb_tables.py`](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/duckdb/snippets/duckdb_tables.py) (Python): Read and append to a Unity Catalog managed Delta table from DuckDB.
  - run: `UNITY_CATALOG_URL=http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog uv run https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/duckdb/snippets/duckdb_tables.py`

DuckDB queries [Unity Catalog](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/what-is-unity-catalog/ "The open-source reference server implementing the Unity Catalog specification.") tables with SQL, appends rows to them, and creates catalog-managed Delta tables. DuckDB's `unity_catalog` extension attaches a catalog as a DuckDB database, and its `delta` extension reads and writes the [Delta](https://delta.io "Open table-format specification: ACID transactions, schema evolution, and time travel over object storage.") files. Appends to a catalog-managed table go through the server, like a Spark write.

> **Prerequisites**
>
> - [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-started/get-docker/) with Compose v2, for the local environment.
> - Unity Catalog 0.7.0, running: [Run a local Unity Catalog server](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/run-local-server/).
> - A Delta table in Unity Catalog, such as `retail.sales.orders` from [Create and update a catalog-managed Delta table](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/tutorials/managed-delta-table/).
> - Table files that DuckDB can reach, such as the local server's [shared folder](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/run-local-server/#share-a-folder-with-the-server).
> - [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/).

## Install the extensions

Open a Python session with DuckDB:

```bash
uv run --with duckdb==2.0.0 python
```

Install and load the `delta` and `unity_catalog` extensions:

`duckdb_tables.py`

```python
import duckdb

con = duckdb.connect()
con.execute("INSTALL delta")
con.execute("LOAD delta")
con.execute("INSTALL unity_catalog")
con.execute("LOAD unity_catalog")
```

## Attach a catalog

Create a secret that holds the server's address and a token, then attach one Unity Catalog catalog as a DuckDB database:

`duckdb_tables.py`

```python
con.execute("""
    CREATE SECRET (
        TYPE unity_catalog,
        TOKEN 'not-used',
        ENDPOINT 'http://localhost:8080'
    )
""")
con.execute("ATTACH 'retail' AS retail (TYPE unity_catalog, DEFAULT_SCHEMA 'sales')")
```

- `ENDPOINT` is the server's base URL, without `/api/2.1/unity-catalog`.
- `TOKEN` is sent as a bearer token. The local server has authorization disabled and accepts any value. On a secured server, use a Unity Catalog access token.
- `DEFAULT_SCHEMA` is the schema DuckDB uses for unqualified table names.

Leave the secret unnamed. With a named secret (`CREATE SECRET uc (...)`), `ATTACH` fails with `Could not resolve hostname`.

## List tables

`duckdb_tables.py`

```python
con.sql("SELECT database, schema, name FROM (SHOW ALL TABLES)").show()
```

```text
┌──────────┬─────────┬─────────┐
│ database │ schema  │  name   │
│ varchar  │ varchar │ varchar │
├──────────┼─────────┼─────────┤
│ retail   │ sales   │ orders  │
└──────────┴─────────┴─────────┘
```

## Query a table

Use three-part names, or just the table name for tables in the default schema:

`duckdb_tables.py`

```python
con.sql("""
    SELECT customer, amount
    FROM retail.sales.orders
    WHERE amount > 5
    ORDER BY order_id
""").show()
```

```text
┌──────────┬───────────────┐
│ customer │    amount     │
│ varchar  │ decimal(10,2) │
├──────────┼───────────────┤
│ ada      │          9.50 │
│ grace    │         20.00 │
└──────────┴───────────────┘
```

DuckDB asks the server for the table's location and for temporary credentials, then reads the Delta files directly from storage. For a catalog-managed table it reads the latest version the server has accepted. DuckDB reads tables with column mapping through Unity Catalog, too.

## Append rows

`INSERT` adds rows to the table:

`duckdb_tables.py`

```python
con.execute("INSERT INTO retail.sales.orders VALUES (4, 'barbara', 12.00)")
```

On a catalog-managed table, DuckDB writes the new data and commit file, then asks the server to accept the commit as the table's next version. From then on, Spark and every other client see the new rows.

DuckDB can't append to a partitioned table that uses column mapping. The insert fails with `Not implemented Error: Inserting into a partitioned Delta table that uses column mapping is not supported`, and the table doesn't change.

## Create, change, and drop tables

`CREATE TABLE` creates a catalog-managed table, and `INSERT` adds its rows:

`duckdb_tables.py`

```python
con.execute("CREATE TABLE retail.sales.returns (order_id BIGINT, reason VARCHAR)")
con.execute("INSERT INTO retail.sales.returns VALUES (4, 'damaged')")
```

The server stages the new table as it does for Spark, so Spark and other clients read it and append to it.

DuckDB can't create a table from a query (`CREATE TABLE … AS SELECT`), update or delete rows, or drop a table. Do those with Spark, as in [Create and update a catalog-managed Delta table](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/tutorials/managed-delta-table/).

## Required privileges

With authorization enabled, reading needs `USE CATALOG` on the catalog, `USE SCHEMA` on the schema, and `SELECT` on the table. Appending also needs `MODIFY` on the table, and creating a table needs `CREATE TABLE` on the schema. Owners have all of these. See [Core concepts](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/uc-basics/#ownership-and-privileges).

## Next steps

- [External tables and catalog-managed Delta tables](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/external-and-managed-tables/) explains why an append from DuckDB is safe next to a Spark writer.
- [DuckDB's Unity Catalog extension documentation](https://duckdb.org/docs/stable/core_extensions/unity_catalog) covers its other secret options and cloud storage.

---

# https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/python-dataframes/

## Companion files

CI-tested scripts that run this page's examples end to end. A script that exits 0 has passed its checks.

They need Unity Catalog 0.7.0 with simulated S3 and PostgreSQL running. To start it (also `environment` in this file's frontmatter):

```bash
curl -fsSL https://unitycatalog.io/docs/env/uc-aws.tar.gz | tar -xz
cd uc-docs-env/uc-aws && docker compose up -d --wait
export AWS_ALLOW_HTTP=true
export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:9000
export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3=http://localhost:9000
export AWS_REGION=us-east-1
export UNITY_CATALOG_URL=http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog
```

- [`daft_tables.py`](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/python-dataframes/snippets/daft_tables.py) (Python): List and read a Unity Catalog table on local storage from Daft.
  - run: `AWS_ALLOW_HTTP=true AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:9000 AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3=http://localhost:9000 AWS_REGION=us-east-1 UNITY_CATALOG_URL=http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog uv run daft_tables.py`
  - save [`_seed.py`](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/python-dataframes/snippets/_seed.py) beside it first; the script imports it
- [`managed_tables_fail.py`](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/python-dataframes/snippets/managed_tables_fail.py) (Python): Pin that Polars, Daft, and pandas (deltalake) can't read or append to a catalog-managed table.
  - run: `AWS_ALLOW_HTTP=true AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:9000 AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3=http://localhost:9000 AWS_REGION=us-east-1 UNITY_CATALOG_URL=http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog uv run https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/python-dataframes/snippets/managed_tables_fail.py`
- [`pandas_tables.py`](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/python-dataframes/snippets/pandas_tables.py) (Python): Read and append to a Unity Catalog table on S3 from pandas, through deltalake.
  - run: `AWS_ALLOW_HTTP=true AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:9000 AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3=http://localhost:9000 AWS_REGION=us-east-1 UNITY_CATALOG_URL=http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog uv run pandas_tables.py`
  - save [`_seed.py`](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/python-dataframes/snippets/_seed.py) beside it first; the script imports it
- [`polars_tables.py`](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/python-dataframes/snippets/polars_tables.py) (Python): List, read, and append to a Unity Catalog table on S3 from Polars.
  - run: `AWS_ALLOW_HTTP=true AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:9000 AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3=http://localhost:9000 AWS_REGION=us-east-1 UNITY_CATALOG_URL=http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog uv run polars_tables.py`
  - save [`_seed.py`](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/python-dataframes/snippets/_seed.py) beside it first; the script imports it

Polars, Daft, and pandas can find [Unity Catalog](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/what-is-unity-catalog/ "The open-source reference server implementing the Unity Catalog specification.") tables by name and read and append to them. Each library looks up the table, asks the server for temporary storage credentials, and then reads or writes the [Delta](https://delta.io "Open table-format specification: ACID transactions, schema evolution, and time travel over object storage.") files directly in storage.

All three work with external Delta tables, through [delta-rs](https://delta-io.github.io/delta-rs/ "Native Rust implementation of the Delta protocol with Python bindings."). For catalog-managed tables, use [Spark](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/configure-spark/) or [DuckDB](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/duckdb/), which commit through the server.

> **Prerequisites**
>
> - [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-started/get-docker/) with Compose v2, for the local environment.
> - Unity Catalog 0.7.0 with simulated S3 and PostgreSQL, running: [Run a local Unity Catalog server](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/run-local-server/#start-the-server-with-simulated-s3).
> - An external Delta table in Unity Catalog, such as `retail.sales.orders`: [Register an existing external table](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/register-external-table/).
> - For tables on S3, an [external location](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/configure-aws-storage/) that covers the table's path.
> - [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/).

The Polars and pandas examples use a table on S3, and the Daft examples a table on local storage, which is what each library is tested with here. The local environment above simulates S3. On real AWS, leave its `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL` and `AWS_ALLOW_HTTP` variables unset.

## Connect to the server

**Polars**

Open a Python session with Polars:

```bash
uv run --with polars==1.44.2 --with deltalake==1.6.6 python
```

`polars_tables.py`

```python
import polars as pl

catalog = pl.Catalog("http://localhost:8080", require_https=False)
```

`pl.Catalog` takes the server's base URL, without `/api/2.1/unity-catalog`. `require_https=False` allows the local `http://` address. On a secured server, pass a Unity Catalog access token as `bearer_token`. Polars marks `pl.Catalog` as unstable, so its API may change in any release.

**Daft**

Open a Python session with Daft:

```bash
uv run --with "daft[unity]==0.7.25" --with tenacity python
```

`daft_tables.py`

```python
import daft
from daft.catalog import Catalog
from daft.catalog.__unity import UnityCatalogClient

client = UnityCatalogClient("http://localhost:8080", token="not-used")
catalog = Catalog.from_unity(client)
```

Pass a `token` even though the local server has authorization disabled. Without one, Daft 0.7.25 sends an empty `Authorization` header and every request fails. On a secured server, use a Unity Catalog access token. Daft 0.7.25 exposes the client only from `daft.catalog.__unity`.

**pandas**

Open a Python session with pandas and `deltalake`:

```bash
uv run --with pandas==2.3.3 --with deltalake==1.6.6 python
```

`pandas_tables.py`

```python
import pandas as pd
from deltalake import DeltaTable, write_deltalake

UNITY = {
    "unity_workspace_url": "http://localhost:8080",
    "unity_access_token": "not-used",
    "unity_allow_http_url": "true",
}
```

pandas has no catalog support of its own. The `deltalake` package resolves `uc://catalog.schema.table` names through these `unity_*` options and returns pandas DataFrames.

## List tables

**Polars**

`polars_tables.py`

```python
for table in catalog.list_tables("retail", "sales"):
    print(table.name, table.table_type, table.storage_location)
```

```text
orders EXTERNAL s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/retail/orders
```

`list_catalogs()` and `list_namespaces(catalog)` list the levels above.

**Daft**

`daft_tables.py`

```python
print(catalog.list_tables("retail.sales"))
```

```text
[Identifier('retail.sales.orders')]
```

`deltalake` can't list tables. With pandas, use the [Python client](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/tutorials/python-client/) to find them.

## Read a table

**Polars**

`polars_tables.py`

```python
orders = catalog.scan_table("retail", "sales", "orders")
print(orders.filter(pl.col("amount") > 5).collect())
```

`scan_table` returns a `LazyFrame`, so filters run as Polars reads the files.

**Daft**

`daft_tables.py`

```python
orders = catalog.get_table("retail.sales.orders").read()
orders.where(daft.col("amount") > 5).show()
```

**pandas**

`pandas_tables.py`

```python
orders = DeltaTable("uc://retail.sales.orders", storage_options=UNITY).to_pandas()
print(orders[orders["amount"] > 5])
```

Each library requests read credentials for the table's location from the server, and then reads the Delta files with them. For how vending works, see [Credential vending](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/credential-vending/).

## Append rows

**Polars**

`polars_tables.py`

```python
new_orders = pl.DataFrame(
    {"order_id": [4], "customer": ["margaret"], "amount": [12.0]}
)
catalog.write_table(new_orders, "retail", "sales", "orders", delta_mode="append")
```

**pandas**

`pandas_tables.py`

```python
new_orders = pd.DataFrame(
    {"order_id": [4], "customer": ["margaret"], "amount": [12.0]}
)
write_deltalake(
    "uc://retail.sales.orders", new_orders, mode="append", storage_options=UNITY
)
```

The library requests read-write credentials, writes new Parquet files, and commits a new version to the table's Delta log. The server isn't involved in the commit, so it doesn't coordinate writers on an external table.

## Other table operations

Create and drop tables with the [Python client](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/tutorials/python-client/) or Spark.

## Required privileges

With authorization enabled, reading needs `USE CATALOG` on the catalog, `USE SCHEMA` on the schema, and `SELECT` on the table. Appending also needs `MODIFY` on the table. Owners have all of these. See [Core concepts](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/uc-basics/#ownership-and-privileges).

## Next steps

- [External tables and catalog-managed Delta tables](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/external-and-managed-tables/) explains why path-based libraries can't use managed tables.
- The [Polars](https://docs.pola.rs/api/python/stable/reference/catalog/index.html), [Daft](https://docs.daft.ai/en/stable/connectors/unity_catalog/), and [delta-rs](https://delta-io.github.io/delta-rs/) documentation cover other storage options and authentication methods.
