# https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/iceberg-rest/

## Companion files

CI-tested scripts that run this page's examples end to end. A script that exits 0 has passed its checks.

They need Unity Catalog 0.7.0 with simulated S3 and PostgreSQL running. To start it (also `environment` in this file's frontmatter):

```bash
curl -fsSL https://unitycatalog.io/docs/env/uc-aws.tar.gz | tar -xz
cd uc-docs-env/uc-aws && docker compose up -d --wait
export AWS_ALLOW_HTTP=true
export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:9000
export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3=http://localhost:9000
export AWS_REGION=us-east-1
export UNITY_CATALOG_URL=http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog
```

- [`datafusion_iceberg.rs`](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/iceberg-rest/snippets/datafusion_iceberg.rs) (Rust): Create, change, and drop an Iceberg table in Unity Catalog from DataFusion in Rust, through
  - run: `cargo add datafusion@55.1 && cargo add iceberg --git https://github.com/apache/iceberg-rust --rev 5b82ab99aeaf50bf4f5b3b776ac9cd6380a5f3e3 && cargo add iceberg-catalog-rest --git https://github.com/apache/iceberg-rust --rev 5b82ab99aeaf50bf4f5b3b776ac9cd6380a5f3e3 && cargo add iceberg-datafusion --git https://github.com/apache/datafusion-iceberg --rev 8979482936eff6509e40c2e4e3bfc1235d965d60 && cargo add iceberg-storage-opendal --git https://github.com/apache/iceberg-rust --rev 5b82ab99aeaf50bf4f5b3b776ac9cd6380a5f3e3 && cargo add reqwest@0.12 --features json && cargo add serde_json@1 && cargo add tokio@1 --features macros,rt-multi-thread && cargo run`, in a new Cargo project with it as `src/main.rs`
- [`duckdb_iceberg.py`](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/iceberg-rest/snippets/duckdb_iceberg.py) (Python): Create, change, and drop an Iceberg table in Unity Catalog from DuckDB, through Iceberg REST.
  - run: `AWS_ALLOW_HTTP=true AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:9000 AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3=http://localhost:9000 AWS_REGION=us-east-1 UNITY_CATALOG_URL=http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog uv run duckdb_iceberg.py`
  - save [`_setup.py`](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/iceberg-rest/snippets/_setup.py) beside it first; the script imports it
- [`pyiceberg_tables.py`](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/iceberg-rest/snippets/pyiceberg_tables.py) (Python): Create, change, and drop an Iceberg table in Unity Catalog from PyIceberg, through Iceberg REST.
  - run: `AWS_ALLOW_HTTP=true AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:9000 AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3=http://localhost:9000 AWS_REGION=us-east-1 UNITY_CATALOG_URL=http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog uv run pyiceberg_tables.py`
  - save [`_setup.py`](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/iceberg-rest/snippets/_setup.py) beside it first; the script imports it
- [`spark_cross_format.py`](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/iceberg-rest/snippets/spark_cross_format.py) (Python): Join a Delta table and an Iceberg table from the same Unity Catalog catalog in one Spark session.
  - run: `AWS_ALLOW_HTTP=true AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:9000 AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3=http://localhost:9000 AWS_REGION=us-east-1 UNITY_CATALOG_URL=http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog uv run spark_cross_format.py`
  - save [`_setup.py`](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/iceberg-rest/snippets/_setup.py) beside it first; the script imports it
- [`spark_iceberg.py`](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/iceberg-rest/snippets/spark_iceberg.py) (Python): Create, change, and drop an Iceberg table in Unity Catalog from Spark, through Iceberg REST.
  - run: `AWS_ALLOW_HTTP=true AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:9000 AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3=http://localhost:9000 AWS_REGION=us-east-1 UNITY_CATALOG_URL=http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog uv run spark_iceberg.py`
  - save [`_setup.py`](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/iceberg-rest/snippets/_setup.py) beside it first; the script imports it

[Unity Catalog](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/what-is-unity-catalog/ "The open-source reference server implementing the Unity Catalog specification.") serves the [Iceberg REST catalog API](https://iceberg.apache.org/rest-catalog-spec/ "Open specification for an Iceberg catalog served over REST: engines use it to create, load, and commit Iceberg tables through any conforming catalog."), so any client that speaks it can create, write, read, rename, and drop [Iceberg](https://iceberg.apache.org "Open table-format specification for huge analytic datasets, with hidden partitioning and snapshot isolation.") tables in a Unity Catalog catalog. The server allocates storage for each new table and vends short-lived credentials for it, so clients never hold bucket keys. Iceberg tables live next to Delta tables in the same schemas, under the same privileges.

> **Prerequisites**
>
> - [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-started/get-docker/) with Compose v2, for the local environment.
> - Unity Catalog 0.7.0 with simulated S3 and PostgreSQL, running: [Run a local Unity Catalog server](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/run-local-server/#start-the-server-with-simulated-s3).
> - A catalog with managed storage on S3, such as `retail`: [Set managed storage for catalogs and schemas on S3](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/managed-storage-s3/).
> - [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/).
> - [Java 17](https://adoptium.net/temurin/releases/?version=17), for Spark.
> - [Rust](https://www.rust-lang.org/tools/install), for DataFusion.

## How Iceberg names map to the catalog

Every client is configured with the same three values:

| Iceberg REST setting | Value                                                                                                                                           |
| -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Catalog URI          | `http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog/iceberg`                                                                                           |
| Warehouse            | The name of one Unity Catalog catalog, here `retail`. A client works with one catalog at a time; configure a second client catalog for another. |
| Token                | A Unity Catalog access token, sent as a bearer token. The local server has authorization disabled and accepts any value.                        |

Inside that catalog, an Iceberg namespace is a Unity Catalog schema, and an Iceberg table is a table whose data source format is `ICEBERG`. Namespaces don't nest. A table created without a location is a managed table under the schema's or catalog's storage root; the server records where it lives and deletes its files when you drop it.

Through this API, the server lists Iceberg tables, and Delta tables only when they carry UniForm Iceberg metadata. Reach other Delta tables with a Delta client, or [with both in one Spark session](#join-delta-and-iceberg-tables-in-spark).

## Connect a client

**Spark**

Open a Python session with PySpark:

```bash
uv run --with pyspark==4.1.0 python
```

`spark_iceberg.py`

```python
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

ICEBERG_SPARK = "org.apache.iceberg:iceberg-spark-runtime-4.1_2.13:1.11.0"
ICEBERG_AWS = "org.apache.iceberg:iceberg-aws-bundle:1.11.0"

spark = (
    SparkSession.builder.appName("uc-iceberg")
    .config("spark.jars.packages", f"{ICEBERG_SPARK},{ICEBERG_AWS}")
    .config(
        "spark.sql.extensions",
        "org.apache.iceberg.spark.extensions.IcebergSparkSessionExtensions",
    )
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.retail", "org.apache.iceberg.spark.SparkCatalog")
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.retail.type", "rest")
    .config(
        "spark.sql.catalog.retail.uri",
        "http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog/iceberg",
    )
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.retail.warehouse", "retail")
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.retail.token", "not-used")
    .config("spark.sql.defaultCatalog", "retail")
    .getOrCreate()
)
```

This is Iceberg's own Spark catalog, not the Unity Catalog connector. The Iceberg runtime is built per Spark minor version, and the AWS bundle adds the S3 file system that reads and writes table files with the credentials the server vends. The `warehouse` setting picks the Unity Catalog catalog. The `retail` in `spark.sql.catalog.retail` is only Spark's name for it, and making it the default catalog lets later statements name tables as `sales.orders`.

**DuckDB**

Open a Python session with DuckDB:

```bash
uv run --with duckdb==2.0.0 python
```

Install and load the `iceberg` extension:

`duckdb_iceberg.py`

```python
import duckdb

con = duckdb.connect()
con.execute("INSTALL iceberg")
con.execute("LOAD iceberg")
con.execute("SET iceberg_use_metadata_log = false")
```

Then create a secret that holds the token and attach the catalog:

`duckdb_iceberg.py`

```python
con.execute("CREATE SECRET uc (TYPE iceberg, TOKEN 'not-used')")
con.execute("""
    ATTACH 'retail' AS retail (
        TYPE iceberg,
        SECRET uc,
        ENDPOINT 'http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog/iceberg'
    )
""")
```

`ATTACH` takes the warehouse, here `retail`. DuckDB uses the credentials the server vends for each table.

Turning off `iceberg_use_metadata_log` avoids an intermittent commit failure on a session's second write to a table.

> **Note**
>
> DuckDB doesn't read `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL`. Against the local environment's simulated S3, point it at the endpoint yourself:
>
> `duckdb_iceberg.py`
>
> ```python
> con.execute("SET s3_endpoint = 'localhost:9000'")
> con.execute("SET s3_use_ssl = false")
> con.execute("SET s3_url_style = 'path'")
> ```
>
> On real AWS, leave these settings out.

**PyIceberg**

Open a Python session with PyIceberg:

```bash
uv run --with "pyiceberg[pyarrow]==0.12.0" python
```

`pyiceberg_tables.py`

```python
import pyarrow as pa
from pyiceberg.catalog import load_catalog

```

`pyiceberg_tables.py`

```python
catalog = load_catalog(
    "retail",
    type="rest",
    uri="http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog/iceberg",
    warehouse="retail",
    token="not-used",
)
```

`load_catalog` takes the client-side name first, then the same three values. PyIceberg uses the credentials the server vends for each table.

> **Note**
>
> PyIceberg doesn't read `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL`. Against the local environment's simulated S3, also export `PYICEBERG_CATALOG__RETAIL__S3__ENDPOINT=http://localhost:9000` before you start Python. The `RETAIL` part is the name you pass to `load_catalog`. On real AWS, leave it unset.

**DataFusion**

Create a Cargo project with [iceberg-rust](https://rust.iceberg.apache.org "Rust implementation of Apache Iceberg with REST catalog and table APIs, and a DataFusion integration.")'s REST catalog, its [DataFusion](https://datafusion.apache.org "Extensible, high-performance query engine in Rust using Apache Arrow.") integration and S3 storage, DataFusion, and the Tokio runtime:

```bash
cargo new iceberg-datafusion && cd iceberg-datafusion
cargo add iceberg-datafusion --git https://github.com/apache/datafusion-iceberg --rev 8979482936eff6509e40c2e4e3bfc1235d965d60
cargo add iceberg iceberg-catalog-rest iceberg-storage-opendal --git https://github.com/apache/iceberg-rust --rev 5b82ab99aeaf50bf4f5b3b776ac9cd6380a5f3e3
cargo add datafusion@55.1
cargo add tokio --features macros,rt-multi-thread
```

The DataFusion integration isn't on crates.io, so the first command adds it from a commit of its repository, and the next two add the iceberg-rust commit and DataFusion release it builds on.

The steps below go into `src/main.rs`, in a `#[tokio::main] async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>`. Run them with `cargo run`. They use these imports:

`datafusion_iceberg.rs`

```rust
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::sync::Arc;

use datafusion::prelude::SessionContext;
use iceberg::{Catalog, CatalogBuilder, NamespaceIdent, TableIdent};
use iceberg_catalog_rest::RestCatalogBuilder;
use iceberg_datafusion::IcebergCatalogProvider;
use iceberg_storage_opendal::OpenDalStorageFactory;
```

`datafusion_iceberg.rs`

```rust
let catalog: Arc<dyn Catalog> = Arc::new(
    RestCatalogBuilder::default()
        .with_storage_factory(Arc::new(OpenDalStorageFactory::S3 {
            customized_credential_load: None,
        }))
        .load(
            "retail",
            HashMap::from([
                (
                    "uri".to_string(),
                    "http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog/iceberg".to_string(),
                ),
                ("warehouse".to_string(), "retail".to_string()),
                ("token".to_string(), "not-used".to_string()),
            ]),
        )
        .await?,
);
let ctx = SessionContext::new();
let provider = IcebergCatalogProvider::try_new(catalog.clone()).await?;
ctx.register_catalog("retail", Arc::new(provider));
```

The REST catalog takes the same three values, and its S3 storage uses the credentials the server vends for each table. `register_catalog` makes the catalog's schemas DataFusion schemas, so SQL names a table `retail.sales.orders`. Keep `catalog` as well: schemas and renames go through it.

## Create a schema

**Spark**

`spark_iceberg.py`

```python
spark.sql("CREATE NAMESPACE staging")
spark.sql("SHOW NAMESPACES").show()
```

**DuckDB**

`duckdb_iceberg.py`

```python
con.execute("CREATE SCHEMA retail.staging")
con.sql(
    "SELECT schema_name FROM duckdb_schemas() WHERE database_name = 'retail'"
).show()
```

**PyIceberg**

`pyiceberg_tables.py`

```python
catalog.create_namespace("staging")
print(catalog.list_namespaces())
```

**DataFusion**

`datafusion_iceberg.rs`

```rust
let staging = NamespaceIdent::new("staging".to_string());
catalog.create_namespace(&staging, HashMap::new()).await?;
for namespace in catalog.list_namespaces(None).await? {
    println!("{namespace}");
}
```

DataFusion SQL has no `CREATE SCHEMA` for an Iceberg catalog, so create the namespace through the catalog. DataFusion lists the schemas when you create the provider; create it again to query tables in the new schema.

The new namespace is an ordinary Unity Catalog schema, `retail.staging`, and other clients see it at once.

## Create a table

**Spark**

`spark_iceberg.py`

```python
spark.sql("""
    CREATE TABLE sales.orders (
        order_id BIGINT,
        customer STRING,
        amount DOUBLE
    ) USING iceberg
""")
```

**DuckDB**

`duckdb_iceberg.py`

```python
con.execute("""
    CREATE TABLE retail.sales.orders (
        order_id BIGINT,
        customer VARCHAR,
        amount DOUBLE
    )
""")
```

**PyIceberg**

`pyiceberg_tables.py`

```python
orders_schema = pa.schema(
    [("order_id", pa.int64()), ("customer", pa.string()), ("amount", pa.float64())]
)
orders = catalog.create_table("sales.orders", schema=orders_schema)
```

**DataFusion**

`datafusion_iceberg.rs`

```rust
ctx.sql(
    "CREATE TABLE retail.sales.orders (
        order_id BIGINT,
        customer VARCHAR,
        amount DOUBLE
    )",
)
.await?
.collect()
.await?;
```

The server creates the table as `MANAGED`, with data source format `ICEBERG`, at a location under the catalog's storage root: `s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/retail/managed/__unitystorage/catalogs/<catalog id>/tables/<table id>`.

## Write and read rows

**Spark**

`spark_iceberg.py`

```python
spark.sql("""
    INSERT INTO sales.orders VALUES
        (1, 'ada', 9.5),
        (2, 'grace', 20.0),
        (3, 'linus', 3.25)
""")
```

`spark_iceberg.py`

```python
spark.sql("SELECT * FROM sales.orders WHERE amount > 5 ORDER BY order_id").show()
```

```text
+--------+--------+------+
|order_id|customer|amount|
+--------+--------+------+
|       1|     ada|   9.5|
|       2|   grace|  20.0|
+--------+--------+------+
```

**DuckDB**

`duckdb_iceberg.py`

```python
con.execute("""
    INSERT INTO retail.sales.orders VALUES
        (1, 'ada', 9.5),
        (2, 'grace', 20.0),
        (3, 'linus', 3.25)
""")
```

`duckdb_iceberg.py`

```python
con.sql("SELECT * FROM retail.sales.orders WHERE amount > 5 ORDER BY order_id").show()
```

```text
┌──────────┬──────────┬────────┐
│ order_id │ customer │ amount │
│  int64   │ varchar  │ double │
├──────────┼──────────┼────────┤
│        1 │ ada      │    9.5 │
│        2 │ grace    │   20.0 │
└──────────┴──────────┴────────┘
```

**PyIceberg**

`pyiceberg_tables.py`

```python
orders.append(
    pa.table(
        {
            "order_id": [1, 2, 3],
            "customer": ["ada", "grace", "linus"],
            "amount": [9.5, 20.0, 3.25],
        },
        schema=orders_schema,
    )
)
```

`pyiceberg_tables.py`

```python
print(orders.scan(row_filter="amount > 5").to_arrow().sort_by("order_id"))
```

```text
pyarrow.Table
order_id: int64
customer: string
amount: double
----
order_id: [[1,2]]
customer: [["ada","grace"]]
amount: [[9.5,20]]
```

**DataFusion**

`datafusion_iceberg.rs`

```rust
ctx.sql(
    "INSERT INTO retail.sales.orders VALUES
        (1, 'ada', 9.5),
        (2, 'grace', 20.0),
        (3, 'linus', 3.25)",
)
.await?
.collect()
.await?;
```

`datafusion_iceberg.rs`

```rust
ctx.sql("SELECT * FROM retail.sales.orders WHERE amount > 5 ORDER BY order_id")
    .await?
    .show()
    .await?;
```

```text
+----------+----------+--------+
| order_id | customer | amount |
+----------+----------+--------+
| 1        | ada      | 9.5    |
| 2        | grace    | 20.0   |
+----------+----------+--------+
```

The client writes data and metadata files with the vended credentials, then asks the server to commit the new snapshot. The server accepts a commit only if the table hasn't changed since the client read it, so concurrent writers can't overwrite each other.

## Update and delete rows

**Spark**

`spark_iceberg.py`

```python
spark.sql("UPDATE sales.orders SET amount = 21.0 WHERE order_id = 2")
spark.sql("DELETE FROM sales.orders WHERE customer = 'linus'")
spark.sql("""
    MERGE INTO sales.orders AS t
    USING (SELECT 4 AS order_id, 'barbara' AS customer, 12.0 AS amount) AS s
    ON t.order_id = s.order_id
    WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *
    WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *
""")
```

`UPDATE`, `DELETE FROM`, and `MERGE INTO` need the Iceberg SQL extensions from the session configuration.

**DuckDB**

`duckdb_iceberg.py`

```python
con.execute("UPDATE retail.sales.orders SET amount = 21.0 WHERE order_id = 2")
con.execute("DELETE FROM retail.sales.orders WHERE customer = 'linus'")
```

**PyIceberg**

`pyiceberg_tables.py`

```python
orders.delete(delete_filter="customer = 'linus'")
orders.overwrite(
    pa.table(
        {"order_id": [2], "customer": ["grace"], "amount": [21.0]},
        schema=orders_schema,
    ),
    overwrite_filter="order_id = 2",
)
```

PyIceberg has no `UPDATE`. Replace the matching rows with `overwrite` and an `overwrite_filter`.

**DataFusion**

DataFusion's Iceberg integration has no `UPDATE` or `DELETE FROM`; its `INSERT INTO` only appends.

## Rename and drop a table

**Spark**

`spark_iceberg.py`

```python
spark.sql("ALTER TABLE sales.orders RENAME TO sales.order_history")
```

`spark_iceberg.py`

```python
spark.sql("DROP TABLE sales.order_history")
spark.sql("DROP NAMESPACE staging")
```

**DuckDB**

`duckdb_iceberg.py`

```python
con.execute("ALTER TABLE retail.sales.orders RENAME TO order_history")
```

`duckdb_iceberg.py`

```python
con.execute("DROP TABLE retail.sales.order_history")
con.execute("DROP SCHEMA retail.staging")
```

**PyIceberg**

`pyiceberg_tables.py`

```python
catalog.rename_table("sales.orders", "sales.order_history")
```

`pyiceberg_tables.py`

```python
catalog.drop_table("sales.order_history")
catalog.drop_namespace("staging")
```

**DataFusion**

`datafusion_iceberg.rs`

```rust
catalog
    .rename_table(
        &TableIdent::from_strs(["sales", "orders"])?,
        &TableIdent::from_strs(["sales", "order_history"])?,
    )
    .await?;
```

`datafusion_iceberg.rs`

```rust
catalog
    .drop_table(&TableIdent::from_strs(["sales", "order_history"])?)
    .await?;
catalog.drop_namespace(&staging).await?;
```

DataFusion SQL has no `ALTER TABLE … RENAME`, so rename through the catalog. DataFusion keeps the table names it has already seen, so drop the renamed table through the catalog too, or create the provider again before you name it in SQL.

A rename keeps the table in its schema. Dropping a managed table removes it from the catalog, and a background worker on the server deletes its files. An external table, one created with an explicit location, keeps its files; the server accepts a purge request for it but leaves the files in place.

Only tables created through Iceberg REST can be dropped through it. Drop a Delta table through Spark's Unity Catalog connector or the [Unity Catalog API](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/tutorials/python-client/).

## Join Delta and Iceberg tables in Spark

One Spark session can hold both kinds of table: register the catalog twice, once through the Unity Catalog connector for Delta tables and once through Iceberg REST for Iceberg tables.

`spark_cross_format.py`

```python
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

PACKAGES = [
    "io.unitycatalog:unitycatalog-spark_4.1_2.13:0.7.0",
    "io.delta:delta-spark_4.1_2.13:4.3.1",
    "org.apache.hadoop:hadoop-aws:3.4.2",
    "org.apache.iceberg:iceberg-spark-runtime-4.1_2.13:1.11.0",
    "org.apache.iceberg:iceberg-aws-bundle:1.11.0",
]

spark = (
    SparkSession.builder.appName("uc-delta-and-iceberg")
    .config("spark.jars.packages", ",".join(PACKAGES))
    .config(
        "spark.sql.extensions",
        "io.delta.sql.DeltaSparkSessionExtension,"
        "org.apache.iceberg.spark.extensions.IcebergSparkSessionExtensions",
    )
    .config(
        "spark.sql.catalog.spark_catalog",
        "org.apache.spark.sql.delta.catalog.DeltaCatalog",
    )
    .config("spark.hadoop.fs.s3.impl", "org.apache.hadoop.fs.s3a.S3AFileSystem")
    # Delta tables, through the Unity Catalog connector.
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.retail", "io.unitycatalog.spark.UCSingleCatalog")
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.retail.uri", "http://localhost:8080")
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.retail.auth.type", "static")
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.retail.auth.token", "not-used")
    # Iceberg tables in the same catalog, through Iceberg REST.
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.retail_iceberg", "org.apache.iceberg.spark.SparkCatalog")
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.retail_iceberg.type", "rest")
    .config(
        "spark.sql.catalog.retail_iceberg.uri",
        "http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog/iceberg",
    )
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.retail_iceberg.warehouse", "retail")
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.retail_iceberg.token", "not-used")
    .getOrCreate()
)
```

The connector needs `hadoop-aws` for `s3://` paths; use the version that matches your Spark's Hadoop libraries (3.4.2 for Spark 4.1). For the connector settings, see [Use Spark with Unity Catalog](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/configure-spark/). Create a table of each kind, then query them together:

`spark_cross_format.py`

```python
spark.sql("CREATE TABLE retail.sales.customers (id BIGINT, name STRING) USING DELTA")
spark.sql("INSERT INTO retail.sales.customers VALUES (1, 'ada'), (2, 'grace')")

spark.sql("""
    CREATE TABLE retail_iceberg.sales.orders (
        order_id BIGINT, customer_id BIGINT, amount DOUBLE
    ) USING iceberg
""")
spark.sql("""
    INSERT INTO retail_iceberg.sales.orders VALUES
        (10, 1, 9.5), (11, 2, 20.0), (12, 1, 1.5)
""")
```

`spark_cross_format.py`

```python
spark.sql("""
    SELECT c.name, sum(o.amount) AS total
    FROM retail.sales.customers AS c
    JOIN retail_iceberg.sales.orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id
    GROUP BY c.name
    ORDER BY c.name
""").show()
```

```text
+-----+-----+
| name|total|
+-----+-----+
|  ada| 11.0|
|grace| 20.0|
+-----+-----+
```

Name each table through the catalog for its format. The connector lists the Iceberg table too, but can't read it, and Iceberg REST doesn't list Delta tables.

## Required privileges

With authorization enabled, the server checks the same privileges as for any other table. Reading needs `USE CATALOG` on the catalog, `USE SCHEMA` on the schema, and `SELECT` on the table. Writing also needs `MODIFY`; without it, the server vends read-only credentials. Creating a table needs `CREATE TABLE` on the schema, and creating a schema needs `CREATE SCHEMA` on the catalog. Owners have all of these. See [Core concepts](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/uc-basics/#ownership-and-privileges).

## Next steps

- [Credential vending](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/credential-vending/) explains how the server scopes the credentials it hands each client.
- [External tables and catalog-managed Delta tables](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/external-and-managed-tables/) covers the Delta side of the same catalog.
- The [Iceberg REST catalog specification](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/blob/apache-iceberg-1.11.0/open-api/rest-catalog-open-api.yaml) lists the endpoints these clients call.

---

# https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/java-client/

## Companion files

CI-tested scripts that run this page's examples end to end. A script that exits 0 has passed its checks.

They need Unity Catalog 0.7.0 running. To start it (also `environment` in this file's frontmatter):

```bash
curl -fsSL https://unitycatalog.io/docs/env/unitycatalog.tar.gz | tar -xz
cd uc-docs-env/unitycatalog && docker compose up -d --wait
export UNITY_CATALOG_URL=http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog
```

- [`JavaClient.java`](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/java-client/snippets/JavaClient.java) (Java): Manage Unity Catalog objects from Java with the unitycatalog-client SDK.
  - run: `jbang JavaClient.java`

The [Unity Catalog Java SDK](https://central.sonatype.com/artifact/io.unitycatalog/unitycatalog-client "Generated synchronous Java client for Unity Catalog REST APIs.") is a synchronous client generated from the [Unity Catalog](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/what-is-unity-catalog/ "The open-source reference server implementing the Unity Catalog specification.") REST API. It has one class per resource (`CatalogsApi`, `SchemasApi`, `TablesApi`, `VolumesApi`, `FunctionsApi`, and others), each with one method per operation, and model classes for the requests and responses. This page builds one client in an application and uses it for the calls most applications make.

> **Prerequisites**
>
> - [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-started/get-docker/) with Compose v2, for the local environment.
> - Unity Catalog 0.7.0, running: [Run a local Unity Catalog server](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/run-local-server/).
> - A JDK, version 11 or later.
> - [JBang](https://www.jbang.dev/download/), to run the example as a single file. In a Maven or Gradle project, add the dependency below instead.

## Add the dependency

The client is published to Maven Central as `io.unitycatalog:unitycatalog-client:0.7.0`. Add it to your build's dependencies, or declare it at the top of a JBang file:

`JavaClient.java`

```java
//JAVA 11+
//DEPS io.unitycatalog:unitycatalog-client:0.7.0
```

Pin the version of the server you run. The client brings Jackson and SLF4J and calls the server with the JDK's own HTTP client.

## Connect to the server

Build one `ApiClient` and create the API classes from it. Java has no interactive shell, so put this and the following steps in your application's `main` method or service setup:

`JavaClient.java`

```java
String token = System.getenv().getOrDefault("UC_TOKEN", "not-checked");
ApiClient client = ApiClientBuilder.create()
    .uri("http://localhost:8080")
    .tokenProvider(TokenProvider.create(Map.of("type", "static", "token", token)))
    .addAppVersion("orders-app", "1.0.0")
    .build();

CatalogsApi catalogs = new CatalogsApi(client);
SchemasApi schemas = new SchemasApi(client);
TablesApi tables = new TablesApi(client);
```

- `uri` is the server's address only. The builder appends the API's base path, `/api/2.1/unity-catalog`.
- The builder requires a token provider. A server with authorization disabled, such as the docs' local one, doesn't check the token, so any value works there. For a server with authorization enabled, pass a token the server issued.
- For OAuth client credentials, call `TokenProvider.create` with `type` set to `oauth`, plus `oauth.uri`, `oauth.clientId`, and `oauth.clientSecret`. The provider gets the token and renews it 30 seconds before it expires. `oauth.scope` defaults to `all-apis`.
- `addAppVersion` adds your application's name and version to the `User-Agent` header the client sends.

The client retries a request up to three times in all, with exponential backoff from 500 ms and random jitter, when the server returns HTTP 429 or the connection fails or times out. It doesn't retry other errors. To change that, pass `.retryPolicy(JitterDelayRetryPolicy.builder().maxAttempts(5).build())` to the builder.

## Create a catalog and a schema

Each create method takes a request model built with chained setters, and returns the created object:

`JavaClient.java`

```java
CatalogInfo catalog = catalogs.createCatalog(new CreateCatalog()
    .name("retail")
    .comment("Order and customer data for the retail team")
    .properties(Map.of("owner_team", "retail-analytics")));
schemas.createSchema(new CreateSchema().name("sales").catalogName("retail"));
```

For updates, renames, and deletes, and the privileges each needs, see [Manage catalogs and schemas](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/manage-catalogs-and-schemas/).

## Page through a list

List methods return one page of results and a `next_page_token`. Pass the token to the next call until it comes back empty. The second argument of `listCatalogs` is the page size, which is `1` here so that paging is visible:

`JavaClient.java`

```java
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
String pageToken = null;
do {
  ListCatalogsResponse page = catalogs.listCatalogs(pageToken, 1);
  page.getCatalogs().forEach(c -> names.add(c.getName()));
  pageToken = page.getNextPageToken();
} while (pageToken != null && !pageToken.isEmpty());
System.out.println(names);
```

`listSchemas` and `listTables` page the same way, but take the page size before the token, after their catalog and schema names.

## Register a table

`createTable` registers a table by name, format, location, and columns. Each column needs a type name, a SQL type, and its JSON in Delta schema form. A small helper builds them:

`JavaClient.java`

```java
static ColumnInfo column(String name, ColumnTypeName type, String sql, String delta, int pos) {
  return new ColumnInfo()
      .name(name)
      .typeName(type)
      .typeText(sql)
      .typeJson("{\"name\":\"" + name + "\",\"type\":\"" + delta
          + "\",\"nullable\":true,\"metadata\":{}}")
      .position(pos)
      .nullable(true);
}
```

`JavaClient.java`

```java
TableInfo orders = tables.createTable(new CreateTable()
    .name("orders")
    .catalogName("retail")
    .schemaName("sales")
    .tableType(TableType.EXTERNAL)
    .dataSourceFormat(DataSourceFormat.DELTA)
    .storageLocation("file:///tmp/uc-docs/retail/orders")
    .columns(List.of(
        column("order_id", ColumnTypeName.LONG, "bigint", "long", 0),
        column("amount", ColumnTypeName.DOUBLE, "double", "double", 1))));
System.out.println(orders.getTableId());
```

Registration is metadata only: point `storageLocation` at an existing Delta table. The server doesn't check that the files are there. See [Register external Delta table](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/register-external-table/).

## Look up objects by name

List the tables in a schema, or get one by its three-level name:

`JavaClient.java`

```java
tables.listTables("retail", "sales", 50, null).getTables()
    .forEach(t -> System.out.println(t.getName() + " " + t.getTableType()));
```

`JavaClient.java`

```java
TableInfo found = tables.getTable("retail.sales.orders", false, false);
System.out.println(found.getStorageLocation());
found.getColumns().forEach(c -> System.out.println(c.getName() + " " + c.getTypeText()));
```

The two `false` arguments of `getTable` are `readStreamingTableAsManaged` and `readMaterializedViewAsManaged`. `getCatalog` and `getSchema` take a name only.

## Handle errors

Every call throws `ApiException` when the server answers with an error. `getCode()` returns the HTTP status, and `getResponseBody()` the JSON error, whose `error_code` names the cause:

`JavaClient.java`

```java
int status = 0;
try {
  tables.getTable("retail.sales.returns", false, false);
} catch (ApiException e) {
  status = e.getCode();
  System.out.println("HTTP " + status + ": " + e.getResponseBody());
}
```

A missing object returns 404, as here with `TABLE_NOT_FOUND`. Deleting a catalog that still holds schemas returns 400 unless you force it.

## Clean up

Delete the catalog with everything in it:

`JavaClient.java`

```java
catalogs.deleteCatalog("retail", true);
```

## Next steps

- To query tables from the JVM, use Spark with the Unity Catalog connector: [Configure Spark for Unity Catalog](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/configure-spark/).
- For the same tasks from Python, see [Manage catalogs and schemas](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/manage-catalogs-and-schemas/).

---

# https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/run-server-with-java/

## Companion files

CI-tested scripts that run this page's examples end to end. A script that exits 0 has passed its checks.

- [`run_server.sh`](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/run-server-with-java/snippets/run_server.sh) (Shell): Run the Unity Catalog server from its Maven artifact with JBang, keep its metadata in an H2 file, and query it. Each region is one step of the page.
  - run: `bash run_server.sh`

The [Unity Catalog](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/what-is-unity-catalog/ "The open-source reference server implementing the Unity Catalog specification.") server is published to Maven Central as a runnable jar, `io.unitycatalog:unitycatalog-server:0.7.0`. [JBang](https://www.jbang.dev) downloads it with its dependencies and starts it, so you can run the server on any machine with a JDK, without Docker or a source checkout. To run it in a container instead, see [Run a local Unity Catalog server](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/run-local-server/).

> **Prerequisites**
>
> - A JDK, version 17 or later.
> - [JBang](https://www.jbang.dev/download/).
> - `curl`, to call the server.

## Start the server

Make a folder for the server and start it from there:

`run_server.sh`

```bash
mkdir -p uc-server && cd uc-server
jbang io.unitycatalog:unitycatalog-server:0.7.0 --port 8080
```

The first start downloads the server's dependencies. The server then runs in the foreground on `http://localhost:8080`, and prints its banner. Stop it with Ctrl+C. To use another port, change `--port`.

The server reads its configuration from `etc/conf/` under the folder it starts in, so always start it from the same folder. On first start it creates the folder and writes:

- `private_key.der`, `public_key.der`, and `key_id.txt`: the key pair the server signs its tokens with.
- `token.txt`: a token for the `admin` user, written again on every start. Clients use it when authorization is enabled. See [Core concepts](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/uc-basics/).
- `certs.json`: the public key, for verifying the server's tokens.

## Check that it's running

In another terminal, list the catalogs:

`run_server.sh`

```bash
curl -s http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog/catalogs
```

A new server has no catalogs: `{"catalogs":[],"next_page_token":null}`. Unlike the container image, it doesn't load the sample catalog `unity`. Create one:

`run_server.sh`

```bash
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog/catalogs \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name": "retail"}'
```

## Keep the metadata between restarts

Without configuration, the server keeps its metadata in an in-memory H2 database, so a restart discards every catalog. To keep it in an H2 file instead, stop the server and write `etc/conf/hibernate.properties` from the folder you started it in:

`run_server.sh`

```bash
cd uc-server
cat > etc/conf/hibernate.properties <<'EOF'
hibernate.connection.driver_class=org.h2.Driver
hibernate.connection.url=jdbc:h2:file:./etc/db/h2db;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1
hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto=update
EOF
```

Start the server again. It creates its tables in `etc/db/` and keeps them across restarts.

For a database other people or servers share, use PostgreSQL. The server artifact doesn't depend on the PostgreSQL JDBC driver, so add `org.postgresql:postgresql` to the server's classpath, then follow [Configure PostgreSQL as the metadata database](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/configure-backend-db/).

## Configure the server

The server reads two more optional files from `etc/conf/`:

- `server.properties`: server settings, such as `server.authorization` (`disable` by default) and the storage credentials described in [Configure AWS storage credentials and external locations](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/configure-aws-storage/). Without the file, every setting takes its default.
- `server.log4j2.properties`: the [Log4j 2](https://logging.apache.org/log4j/2.x/manual/configuration.html) configuration. Without it, the server logs nothing beyond its banner and errors.

Restart the server after you change a file.

## Next steps

- Connect an application: [Use the Java client in an application](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/java-client/).

---

# https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/configure-backend-db/

## Companion files

CI-tested scripts that run this page's examples end to end. A script that exits 0 has passed its checks.

They need Unity Catalog 0.7.0 with simulated S3 and PostgreSQL running. To start it (also `environment` in this file's frontmatter):

```bash
curl -fsSL https://unitycatalog.io/docs/env/uc-aws.tar.gz | tar -xz
cd uc-docs-env/uc-aws && docker compose up -d --wait
export AWS_ALLOW_HTTP=true
export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:9000
export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3=http://localhost:9000
export AWS_REGION=us-east-1
export UNITY_CATALOG_URL=http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog
```

- [`backend_db.sh`](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/configure-backend-db/snippets/backend_db.sh) (Shell): Run the local server on PostgreSQL and check that its metadata survives.
  - run: `bash backend_db.sh` from `uc-docs-env/uc-aws`

A [Unity Catalog](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/what-is-unity-catalog/ "The open-source reference server implementing the Unity Catalog specification.") server stores catalogs, schemas, tables, volumes, functions, models, and credentials in a relational database. By default, this is an H2 file inside the server, so the metadata is lost with the container. To keep it in PostgreSQL, mount one `hibernate.properties` file into the server. The official image already includes the PostgreSQL JDBC driver, and the server creates its tables on first start.

> **Prerequisites**
>
> - [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-started/get-docker/) with Compose v2, for the local environment.
> - Unity Catalog 0.7.0 with simulated S3 and PostgreSQL, running: [Run a local Unity Catalog server](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/run-local-server/#start-the-server-with-simulated-s3).
> - A PostgreSQL database that the server can reach, and a role that owns it. This page uses PostgreSQL 16.

## Create the database

Create a role and a database it owns. The server needs to create and alter tables in the database, so the owner is the simplest role to use:

`create-database.sql`

```sql
-- Run as a PostgreSQL superuser or a role with CREATEROLE and CREATEDB.
CREATE ROLE unitycatalog LOGIN PASSWORD 'change-me';
CREATE DATABASE unitycatalog OWNER unitycatalog;
```

## Point the server at PostgreSQL

The server reads `etc/conf/hibernate.properties`, relative to its working directory. In the container that's `/home/unitycatalog/etc/conf/hibernate.properties`. Replace the file with one that names your database:

`hibernate.properties`

```properties
hibernate.connection.driver_class=org.postgresql.Driver
hibernate.connection.url=jdbc:postgresql://db.example.com:5432/unitycatalog?sslmode=require
hibernate.connection.username=unitycatalog
hibernate.connection.password=change-me
hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto=update
hibernate.archive.autodetection=class
hibernate.show_sql=false
```

| Key                                                              | What it sets                                                                                                                       |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `hibernate.connection.driver_class`                              | The JDBC driver. `org.postgresql.Driver` ships in the image.                                                                       |
| `hibernate.connection.url`                                       | The JDBC URL. Add `sslmode` and other [pgJDBC options](https://jdbc.postgresql.org/documentation/use/) as query parameters.        |
| `hibernate.connection.username`, `hibernate.connection.password` | The role from the previous step.                                                                                                   |
| `hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto`                                         | `update` makes the server create missing tables and columns at startup. Keep it: the server has no separate schema migration tool. |
| `hibernate.archive.autodetection`, `hibernate.show_sql`          | The image's defaults.                                                                                                              |

The file replaces the image's own `hibernate.properties`, so write all of these keys, not only the ones you change. With Docker, bind-mount it read-only over the path above. On Kubernetes, mount it from a Secret, because it holds the password. Then restart the server.

If you run the server from a release tarball or a source build instead of the image, also put the PostgreSQL JDBC driver on the server's classpath, as the upstream [deployment guide](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/blob/v0.7.0/docs/server/deployment.md) describes.

A server that can't reach the database doesn't start. It exits with `Exception during creation of SessionFactory` and the database's reason, for example `FATAL: password authentication failed for user "unitycatalog"`.

> **Warning**
>
> A server whose `server.properties` sets `server.env=test` ignores `hibernate.properties` and keeps its metadata in memory. Use `dev` or leave it unset.

## Try it on the local server

The docs' environment with simulated S3 keeps its metadata in PostgreSQL. From the `uc-docs-env/uc-aws` folder, start it instead of the default server:

`backend_db.sh`

```bash
docker compose up -d --wait
```

It runs the server next to a `db` PostgreSQL service, with its data in the `postgres-data` volume. The server's `hibernate.properties` names that database:

`modules/unity-catalog/secrets/hibernate.properties`

```properties
# Generated by trestle. Unity Catalog keeps its metadata in PostgreSQL instead of the image's
# in-container H2 file, so catalogs survive a new container. This file replaces the image's own
# hibernate.properties, so it writes every key. The image bundles the PostgreSQL JDBC driver.
hibernate.connection.driver_class=org.postgresql.Driver
hibernate.connection.url=jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/unitycatalog
hibernate.connection.username=postgres
hibernate.connection.password=postgres
# The server has no separate migration tool: `update` creates missing tables and columns at
# startup.
hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto=update
hibernate.archive.autodetection=class
hibernate.show_sql=false
```

The server starts with an empty metastore. The sample catalog `unity` lives in the image's H2 file, so it isn't there.

## Check that metadata survives a new container

Define the `uc` alias from [Run the `uc` CLI](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/run-local-server/#run-the-uc-cli) and create a catalog:

`backend_db.sh`

```bash
uc catalog create --name persisted --comment "Survives a new server container"
```

Replace the server container with a new one, then read the catalog back:

`backend_db.sh`

```bash
docker compose up -d --wait --force-recreate unitycatalog
uc catalog get --name persisted --output jsonPretty
```

The catalog is still there. On the default H2 server, the new container would start from the image's H2 file, without it. `docker compose down` followed by `up` keeps the metadata too, because it removes the containers but not the `postgres-data` volume.

The metadata is ordinary PostgreSQL tables, one per object type, named `uc_catalogs`, `uc_schemas`, `uc_tables`, and so on:

`backend_db.sh`

```bash
docker compose exec db \
  psql -U postgres -d unitycatalog -c 'SELECT name, comment FROM uc_catalogs'
```

Read these tables to inspect or back up the metastore, but change objects only through the server's API. The server keeps related rows consistent, and direct writes bypass that.

## Back up and upgrade

Back up the database with the usual PostgreSQL tools. On the local stack:

`backend_db.sh`

```bash
docker compose exec db \
  pg_dump -U postgres unitycatalog > uc-metadata.sql
```

Take a backup before you upgrade the server. On its first start, a new release adds the tables and columns it needs to the database, and nothing reverses that change. To roll back, restore the backup and start the old release.

The backup holds metadata only. Table and volume data stays in its storage locations.

To move from the default H2 database, recreate your catalogs and their contents through the API, or register existing external tables again. There's no export from H2.

## Reset the local metadata

To start over on the local stack, remove the containers and the `postgres-data` volume:

`backend_db.sh`

```bash
docker compose down -v
```

> **Danger**
>
> `down -v` deletes every catalog, schema, table, volume, and credential that the server stored, and the simulated S3 bucket's files. Files the tables point to elsewhere stay where they are, but the server no longer knows about them.

## Next steps

- [Run a local Unity Catalog server](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/run-local-server/) covers the other variants of the local environment.
- [Manage catalogs and schemas](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/manage-catalogs-and-schemas/) to fill the new metastore.

---

# https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/configure-aws-storage/

## Companion files

CI-tested scripts that run this page's examples end to end. A script that exits 0 has passed its checks.

They need Unity Catalog 0.7.0 with simulated S3 and PostgreSQL running. To start it (also `environment` in this file's frontmatter):

```bash
curl -fsSL https://unitycatalog.io/docs/env/uc-aws.tar.gz | tar -xz
cd uc-docs-env/uc-aws && docker compose up -d --wait
export AWS_ALLOW_HTTP=true
export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:9000
export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3=http://localhost:9000
export AWS_REGION=us-east-1
export UNITY_CATALOG_URL=http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog
```

- [`aws_storage.py`](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/configure-aws-storage/snippets/aws_storage.py) (Python): Register an S3 storage credential and external location, and check vending.
  - run: `AWS_ALLOW_HTTP=true AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:9000 AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3=http://localhost:9000 AWS_REGION=us-east-1 UNITY_CATALOG_URL=http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog uv run https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/configure-aws-storage/snippets/aws_storage.py`
- [`aws_storage.sh`](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/configure-aws-storage/snippets/aws_storage.sh) (Shell): Register an S3 storage credential and external location with the uc CLI, and check vending.
  - run: `bash aws_storage.sh` from `uc-docs-env/uc-aws`

A [Unity Catalog](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/what-is-unity-catalog/ "The open-source reference server implementing the Unity Catalog specification.") server governs access to Amazon S3 through storage credentials and external locations, and it never hands out long-lived keys. When an authorized client needs data, the server assumes an IAM role through AWS STS and returns credentials that expire after an hour and are scoped to the path the client asked for. For why this matters, see [Credential vending](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/credential-vending/).

Three IAM principals and two catalog objects are involved:

| Name on this page                 | What it is                                                                     | Where it lives                     |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------- |
| Master role `uc-master`           | The identity the server runs as. It may only assume storage roles.             | IAM, attached to the server's host |
| Storage role `uc-storage-lake`    | Reads and writes one bucket or prefix. It trusts the master role.              | IAM                                |
| Storage credential `lake_storage` | Records the storage role's ARN, plus an external ID that the server generates. | Unity Catalog                      |
| External location `lake`          | Binds `s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/lake` to the storage credential.               | Unity Catalog                      |

When a client requests access to a path under `s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/lake`, the server finds the matching external location, assumes its credential's storage role as the master role with the credential's external ID, and attaches a session policy that narrows access to the requested path and operation.

> **Prerequisites**
>
> - [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-started/get-docker/) with Compose v2, for the local environment.
> - Unity Catalog 0.7.0 with simulated S3 and PostgreSQL, running: [Run a local Unity Catalog server](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/run-local-server/#start-the-server-with-simulated-s3).
> - In AWS, permission to create IAM roles and policies, and to edit the bucket's policy if it has one.
> - [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/), for the Python examples.

To try the steps without an AWS account, use the local environment above with simulated S3. It runs the server's real AWS code path, but it doesn't check trust policies or external IDs, so do the IAM steps for real on AWS.

## Set up the client

Set up the client for your interface:

**Python SDK**

Start Python with the SDK:

```bash
uv run --with unitycatalog-client==0.7.0 --with obstore==0.11.1 python -m asyncio
```

`aws_storage.py`

```python
from obstore.store import from_url
from unitycatalog.client import (
    ApiClient,
    AwsIamRoleRequest,
    Configuration,
    CreateCredentialRequest,
    CreateExternalLocation,
    CredentialPurpose,
    CredentialsApi,
    ExternalLocationsApi,
    GenerateTemporaryPathCredential,
    PathOperation,
    TemporaryCredentialsApi,
    UpdateCredentialRequest,
    UpdateExternalLocation,
)

config = Configuration(host="http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog")
```

Create the API objects from an open client: `async with ApiClient(config) as api: credentials = CredentialsApi(api)`.

**CLI**

`aws_storage.sh`

```bash
uc() { docker exec unitycatalog bin/uc "$@"; }
UC=http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog
```

The CLI connects to `http://localhost:8080` by default. Pass `--server` and `--auth_token` to reach a different server.

## Run the server as a master role

Create an IAM role for the server, for example `uc-master`, with a permission policy that allows only `sts:AssumeRole` on your storage roles. A name prefix keeps the policy stable as you add storage roles:

`uc-master permission policy`

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "AssumeUnityCatalogStorageRoles",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRole",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/uc-storage-*"
    }
  ]
}
```

Attach the role to wherever the server runs: an EC2 instance profile, an ECS task role, or an EKS service account through IRSA or EKS Pod Identity. Then set the role's ARN and region in `server.properties`:

`server.properties (on AWS)`

```properties
# Unity Catalog running on AWS as the master role.
aws.masterRoleArn=arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/uc-master
aws.region=us-east-1
```

Leave `aws.accessKey` and `aws.secretKey` unset. The server then signs its STS calls through the AWS SDK's default credential chain, which picks up the attached role. `aws.masterRoleArn` doesn't select an identity. The server reports it to whoever creates a storage credential, as the principal that the storage role must trust, so it must match the role the server actually runs as.

The server reads each key from a JVM system property first, then from an environment variable with the same name (for example `aws.region`), then from `server.properties`. If `aws.region` is unset, the server uses the AWS SDK's region chain, then the global STS endpoint.

> **Note**
>
> Use exactly these key names. The `aws.s3.masterRoleArn`-style spellings in the upstream `docs/server/aws.md` are silently ignored by the server.

### Run outside AWS

On premises, prefer [IAM Roles Anywhere](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/rolesanywhere/latest/userguide/introduction.html): it gives the host temporary credentials for the master role through the same default credential chain, so the configuration above doesn't change. If that isn't possible, use an IAM user as the master identity. Grant it the same policy, set `aws.masterRoleArn` to the user's ARN, and pass its keys in `aws.accessKey` and `aws.secretKey` (or the standard `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` variables). The local stack does this, with its simulated S3 keys.

## Create a storage credential

First create the storage role in IAM, for example `uc-storage-lake`. Give it a permission policy on the bucket and prefix it serves. A temporary trust policy is enough for now; you replace it once the server has generated the external ID.

`uc-storage-lake permission policy`

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "ReadWriteObjects",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "s3:GetObject",
        "s3:GetObjectVersion",
        "s3:PutObject",
        "s3:DeleteObject",
        "s3:AbortMultipartUpload",
        "s3:ListMultipartUploadParts"
      ],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::amzn-s3-demo-bucket/lake/*"
    },
    {
      "Sid": "ListBucket",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "s3:ListBucket",
        "s3:ListBucketMultipartUploads",
        "s3:GetBucketLocation"
      ],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::amzn-s3-demo-bucket"
    }
  ]
}
```

The server narrows each vended credential to object reads (`s3:GetO*`) and prefix-scoped `s3:ListBucket`, or for writes, also `s3:PutO*`, `s3:DeleteO*`, and the multipart actions. Actions the storage role lacks stay denied, so grant everything your engines need. Engines such as Spark may also call `s3:GetBucketLocation`.

Then register the role with Unity Catalog:

**Python SDK**

`aws_storage.py`

```python
cred = await credentials.create_credential(
    CreateCredentialRequest(
        name="lake_storage",
        purpose=CredentialPurpose.STORAGE,
        aws_iam_role=AwsIamRoleRequest(
            role_arn="arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/uc-storage-lake"
        ),
        comment="Read/write on s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/lake",
    )
)
# Put both values in the storage role's trust policy.
print(cred.aws_iam_role.unity_catalog_iam_arn)
print(cred.aws_iam_role.external_id)
```

**CLI**

`aws_storage.sh`

```bash
uc credential create --name lake_storage \
  --aws_iam_role_arn arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/uc-storage-lake \
  --comment "Read/write on s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/lake" \
  --output jsonPretty
```

The response's `aws_iam_role` holds three values: `role_arn` (the storage role), `unity_catalog_iam_arn` (the server's `aws.masterRoleArn`), and `external_id`, a UUID the server generated for this credential.

**Required privileges:** ownership of the metastore, or `CREATE STORAGE
CREDENTIAL` on it.

## Update the storage role's trust policy

Replace the storage role's trust policy so that only the master role can assume it, and only with this credential's external ID. The external ID stops another tenant of the same server from pointing their own credential at your role.

`uc-storage-lake trust policy`

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {
        "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/uc-master"
      },
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRole",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "sts:ExternalId": "EXTERNAL_ID_FROM_THE_CREDENTIAL"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

Substitute `unity_catalog_iam_arn` for the principal and `external_id` for `EXTERNAL_ID_FROM_THE_CREDENTIAL`. If the master identity is an IAM user, use the user's ARN as the principal.

## Create an external location

An external location makes the server use the credential for every path under its URL:

**Python SDK**

`aws_storage.py`

```python
location = await locations.create_external_location(
    CreateExternalLocation(
        name="lake",
        url="s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/lake",
        credential_name="lake_storage",
    )
)
print(location.url, location.credential_name)
```

**CLI**

`aws_storage.sh`

```bash
uc external_location create --name lake \
  --url s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/lake \
  --credential_name lake_storage \
  --output jsonPretty
```

External locations can't overlap. The server rejects a URL that equals, contains, or falls inside another external location's URL, with `Cannot accept an external location that duplicates or overlaps with existing external location`. Use one location per prefix that has its own storage role.

**Required privileges:** ownership of the metastore; or `CREATE EXTERNAL
LOCATION` on the metastore plus ownership of, or `CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION` on, the storage credential.

## Check that the server vends credentials

Ask for temporary credentials on a path under the location. A successful response proves the whole chain: the server's identity, the trust policy, the external ID, and the storage role's access.

**Python SDK**

The example writes and lists a file with the vended keys:

`aws_storage.py`

```python
vended = await TemporaryCredentialsApi(api).generate_temporary_path_credentials(
    GenerateTemporaryPathCredential(
        url="s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/lake/landing",
        operation=PathOperation.PATH_READ_WRITE,
    )
)
aws = vended.aws_temp_credentials
store = from_url(
    vended.url,
    access_key_id=aws.access_key_id,
    secret_access_key=aws.secret_access_key,
    session_token=aws.session_token,
    region="us-east-1",
)
await obstore.put_async(store, "hello.txt", b"vended by Unity Catalog\n")
print([meta["path"] for meta in await obstore.list(store).collect_async()])
```

**CLI**

The `uc` CLI has no command for this, so call the REST API:

`aws_storage.sh`

```bash
curl -s -X POST "$UC/temporary-path-credentials" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"url": "s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/lake/landing", "operation": "PATH_READ"}'
```

To use the keys with the AWS CLI, export `access_key_id`, `secret_access_key`, and `session_token` as `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, and `AWS_SESSION_TOKEN`.

The credentials reach only the requested path. A write to `s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/lake/curated` with keys vended for `s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/lake/landing` is denied. If the request fails with `AccessDenied` from STS, check the trust policy and the external ID first. Tables and volumes use the same mechanism. Their credential endpoints resolve the object's storage location to its external location.

**Required privileges:** for a path that no table, volume, or registered model owns, ownership of the metastore or of the external location, or `READ FILES` on the location (`PATH_READ`) or both `READ FILES` and `WRITE FILES` (`PATH_READ_WRITE`). For a path inside a table or volume, the usual privileges on that object apply instead, such as `SELECT` on a table or `READ VOLUME` on a volume.

## View storage credentials and external locations

**Python SDK**

`aws_storage.py`

```python
info = await credentials.get_credential(name="lake_storage")
print(info.aws_iam_role.role_arn)
listed = await locations.list_external_locations()
print([(loc.name, loc.url) for loc in listed.external_locations or []])
```

**CLI**

`aws_storage.sh`

```bash
uc credential get --name lake_storage --output jsonPretty
uc external_location list --output jsonPretty
```

The CLI's `credential` and `external_location` commands take the flags `--name`, `--aws_iam_role_arn`, `--url`, `--credential_name`, `--comment`, `--new_name`, and `--force`. Their `--help` pages crash.

**Required privileges:** ownership of the metastore, or ownership of (or `CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION` on) the credential. For an external location: ownership, or any of `READ FILES`, `WRITE FILES`, `CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE`, `CREATE EXTERNAL VOLUME`, and `CREATE MANAGED STORAGE` on it.

## Update a credential or external location

To move a credential to a different storage role, update its role ARN:

**Python SDK**

`aws_storage.py`

```python
updated = await credentials.update_credential(
    name="lake_storage",
    update_credential_request=UpdateCredentialRequest(
        aws_iam_role=AwsIamRoleRequest(
            role_arn="arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/uc-storage-lake-v2"
        ),
    ),
)
print(updated.aws_iam_role.external_id)  # a new ID: update the trust policy
```

**CLI**

`aws_storage.sh`

```bash
uc credential update --name lake_storage \
  --aws_iam_role_arn arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/uc-storage-lake-v2 \
  --output jsonPretty
```

> **Warning**
>
> Changing the role ARN generates a new `external_id`. Vending fails until the new storage role's trust policy names the new ID. Update the trust policy right after the credential. A comment or name change keeps the ID.

Update an external location's comment, name, credential, or URL the same way:

**Python SDK**

`aws_storage.py`

```python
await locations.update_external_location(
    name="lake",
    update_external_location=UpdateExternalLocation(
        comment="Landing and curated data"
    ),
)
```

**CLI**

`aws_storage.sh`

```bash
uc external_location update --name lake \
  --comment "Landing and curated data" \
  --output jsonPretty
```

> **Warning**
>
> The server doesn't check what lives under a location before it accepts a new URL. Tables, volumes, and managed storage roots under the old URL lose their credential, and vending for them fails with `FAILED_PRECONDITION`. Before you change a URL, create the new location alongside the old one if the prefixes don't overlap, and move the data first.

**Required privileges:** for a credential, ownership of it or of the metastore. For an external location, ownership of the metastore, or ownership of the location plus ownership of (or `CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION` on) any new credential.

## Delete an external location and credential

Delete the location first, then the credential:

**Python SDK**

`aws_storage.py`

```python
await locations.delete_external_location(name="lake")
await credentials.delete_credential(name="lake_storage")
```

**CLI**

`aws_storage.sh`

```bash
uc external_location delete --name lake
uc credential delete --name lake_storage
```

An external location can't be deleted while a table, volume, or registered model is stored under it. Catalog and schema storage roots don't count. A credential can't be deleted while an external location uses it. `force` skips these checks. Deleting either object removes only the catalog entry. The data in S3 and the IAM roles stay.

> **Danger**
>
> Always delete the location before its credential. Force-deleting a credential that a location still uses breaks every list of external locations. To recover, force-delete the location by name: `uc external_location delete --name <name> --force true`.

**Required privileges:** ownership of the object or of the metastore.

## Next steps

- [Set managed storage for catalogs and schemas on S3](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/managed-storage-s3/) to put managed tables and volumes under this external location.
- [Configure Spark to use Unity Catalog](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/configure-spark/): Spark needs `hadoop-aws` on the classpath to use vended S3 credentials.
- [Manage volumes](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/manage-volumes/) with `s3://` locations under the external location.

# https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/managed-storage-s3/

## Companion files

CI-tested scripts that run this page's examples end to end. A script that exits 0 has passed its checks.

They need Unity Catalog 0.7.0 with simulated S3 and PostgreSQL running. To start it (also `environment` in this file's frontmatter):

```bash
curl -fsSL https://unitycatalog.io/docs/env/uc-aws.tar.gz | tar -xz
cd uc-docs-env/uc-aws && docker compose up -d --wait
export AWS_ALLOW_HTTP=true
export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:9000
export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3=http://localhost:9000
export AWS_REGION=us-east-1
export UNITY_CATALOG_URL=http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog
```

- [`managed_storage.py`](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/managed-storage-s3/snippets/managed_storage.py) (Python): Give a catalog and a schema S3 storage roots and see where managed data lands.
  - run: `AWS_ALLOW_HTTP=true AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:9000 AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3=http://localhost:9000 AWS_REGION=us-east-1 UNITY_CATALOG_URL=http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog uv run https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/managed-storage-s3/snippets/managed_storage.py`
- [`managed_storage.sh`](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/managed-storage-s3/snippets/managed_storage.sh) (Shell): Give a catalog and a schema S3 storage roots with the uc CLI and see where managed data lands.
  - run: `bash managed_storage.sh` from `uc-docs-env/uc-aws`

A storage root on a catalog or schema tells [Unity Catalog](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/what-is-unity-catalog/ "The open-source reference server implementing the Unity Catalog specification.") where to put managed tables and volumes. When you create a managed object, you don't give it a location. The server allocates one under the schema's storage root or, if the schema has none, under the catalog's. On S3, that root must lie inside an [external location](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/configure-aws-storage/), because the external location's storage credential is what the server uses to vend access to the managed data. For the difference between managed and external objects, see [External tables and catalog-managed Delta tables](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/external-and-managed-tables/).

> **Prerequisites**
>
> - [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-started/get-docker/) with Compose v2, for the local environment.
> - Unity Catalog 0.7.0 with simulated S3 and PostgreSQL, running: [Run a local Unity Catalog server](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/run-local-server/#start-the-server-with-simulated-s3).
> - A storage credential and an external location: [Configure AWS storage credentials and external locations](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/configure-aws-storage/).
> - [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/), for the Python examples.

## Set up the client

Set up the client for your interface:

**Python SDK**

Start Python with the SDK:

```bash
uv run --with unitycatalog-client==0.7.0 --with obstore==0.11.1 python -m asyncio
```

`managed_storage.py`

```python
from obstore.store import from_url
from unitycatalog.client import (
    ApiClient,
    AwsIamRoleRequest,
    CatalogsApi,
    Configuration,
    CreateCatalog,
    CreateCredentialRequest,
    CreateExternalLocation,
    CreateSchema,
    CreateVolumeRequestContent,
    CredentialPurpose,
    CredentialsApi,
    ExternalLocationsApi,
    GenerateTemporaryVolumeCredential,
    SchemasApi,
    TemporaryCredentialsApi,
    VolumeOperation,
    VolumesApi,
    VolumeType,
)

config = Configuration(host="http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog")
```

**CLI**

`managed_storage.sh`

```bash
uc() { docker exec unitycatalog bin/uc "$@"; }
```

The examples use an external location `lake` on `s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/lake`:

**Python SDK**

`managed_storage.py`

```python
await CredentialsApi(api).create_credential(
    CreateCredentialRequest(
        name="lake_storage",
        purpose=CredentialPurpose.STORAGE,
        aws_iam_role=AwsIamRoleRequest(
            role_arn="arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/uc-storage-lake"
        ),
    )
)
await ExternalLocationsApi(api).create_external_location(
    CreateExternalLocation(
        name="lake",

uc credential create --name lake_storage \
  --aws_iam_role_arn arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/uc-storage-lake
uc external_location create --name lake \
  --url s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/lake --credential_name lake_storage
```

## Create a catalog with a storage root

Pass `storage_root` when you create the catalog. The server appends its own prefix and the catalog's ID, and returns the result as `storage_location`:

**Python SDK**

`managed_storage.py`

```python
sales = await CatalogsApi(api).create_catalog(
    CreateCatalog(
        name="sales", storage_root="s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/lake/sales"
    )
)
print(sales.storage_location)
# s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/lake/sales/__unitystorage/catalogs/<catalog id>
```

**CLI**

`managed_storage.sh`

```bash
uc catalog create --name sales \
  --storage_root s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/lake/sales \
  --output jsonPretty
```

The root can be the external location's URL or any path below it. Several catalogs can share one root, since each gets its own ID-named directory.

The root is fixed when the catalog is created. The update API has no `storage_root` field. To move managed data, create a new catalog and copy it.

**Required privileges:** ownership of the metastore or `CREATE CATALOG` on it, plus ownership of the external location or `CREATE MANAGED STORAGE` on it.

## Give a schema its own storage root

A schema without a root uses its catalog's. Give a schema its own root when its data belongs in a different prefix, for example one with a different storage role or retention policy:

**Python SDK**

`managed_storage.py`

```python
schemas = SchemasApi(api)
await schemas.create_schema(CreateSchema(name="raw", catalog_name="sales"))
curated = await schemas.create_schema(
    CreateSchema(
        name="curated",
        catalog_name="sales",
        storage_root="s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/lake/curated",
    )
)
print(curated.storage_location)
# s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/lake/curated/__unitystorage/schemas/<schema id>
```

**CLI**

`managed_storage.sh`

```bash
uc schema create --catalog sales --name raw
uc schema create --catalog sales --name curated \
  --storage_root s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/lake/curated \
  --output jsonPretty
```

A schema's root doesn't have to be under its catalog's root. Here `curated` uses a sibling prefix inside the same external location.

**Required privileges:** ownership of the catalog, or `USE CATALOG` and `CREATE SCHEMA` on it. For a root, also ownership of the external location or `CREATE MANAGED STORAGE` on it.

## Create managed objects

Create a managed volume without a location, and the server picks the nearest root:

**Python SDK**

`managed_storage.py`

```python
volumes = VolumesApi(api)
drops = await volumes.create_volume(
    CreateVolumeRequestContent(
        catalog_name="sales",
        schema_name="raw",
        name="drops",
        volume_type=VolumeType.MANAGED,
    )
)
reports = await volumes.create_volume(
    CreateVolumeRequestContent(
        catalog_name="sales",
        schema_name="curated",
        name="reports",
        volume_type=VolumeType.MANAGED,
    )
)
print(drops.storage_location)  # under the catalog's root
print(reports.storage_location)  # under the schema's root
```

**CLI**

`managed_storage.sh`

```bash
uc volume create --full_name sales.raw.drops --volume_type MANAGED --output jsonPretty
uc volume create --full_name sales.curated.reports --volume_type MANAGED --output jsonPretty
```

Managed paths have these forms:

| Object's schema              | Managed volume path                                                       |
| ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Has no root (`sales.raw`)    | `<catalog root>/__unitystorage/catalogs/<catalog id>/volumes/<volume id>` |
| Has a root (`sales.curated`) | `<schema root>/__unitystorage/schemas/<schema id>/volumes/<volume id>`    |

Managed tables follow the same pattern with `tables/<table id>`. Engines create them through the catalog. See [Create and update a catalog-managed Delta table](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/tutorials/managed-delta-table/).

Clients reach managed data with vended credentials, the same way as for external data:

**Python SDK**

`managed_storage.py`

```python
vended = await TemporaryCredentialsApi(
    api
).generate_temporary_volume_credentials(
    GenerateTemporaryVolumeCredential(
        volume_id=reports.volume_id, operation=VolumeOperation.WRITE_VOLUME
    )
)
aws = vended.aws_temp_credentials
store = from_url(
    vended.url,
    access_key_id=aws.access_key_id,
    secret_access_key=aws.secret_access_key,
    session_token=aws.session_token,
    region="us-east-1",
)
await obstore.put_async(
    store, "2026-10/daily.csv", b"day,total\n2026-10-01,42\n"
)
```

**CLI**

The `uc` CLI can't vend credentials. Use the Python SDK or the REST API `POST /temporary-volume-credentials`.

The `__unitystorage` prefix belongs to the server. An external table or volume whose location contains it is rejected with `Input path '…' contains managed storage prefix __unitystorage.`:

**Python SDK**

The example script checks this rejection in `_check_reserved_prefix`.

**CLI**

`managed_storage.sh`

```bash
uc volume create --full_name sales.raw.sneaky --volume_type EXTERNAL \
  --storage_location s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/lake/sales/__unitystorage/sneaky
```

> **Warning**
>
> Check each root against `external_location list` before you use it. With authorization enabled, the server rejects a root outside every external location. With authorization disabled, as on the local server, it accepts the root, and credential requests for its objects fail later.

## Delete a catalog with managed storage

**Python SDK**

`managed_storage.py`

```python
await CatalogsApi(api).delete_catalog(name="sales", force=True)
```

**CLI**

`managed_storage.sh`

```bash
uc catalog delete --name sales --force true
```

`force` deletes the catalog's schemas and everything in them. Deleting the catalog doesn't delete the external location or the storage credential.

**Required privileges:** ownership of the catalog or of the metastore.
