# https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/delta-api/

## Companion files

CI-tested scripts that run this page's examples end to end. A script that exits 0 has passed its checks.

They need Unity Catalog 0.7.0 running. To start it (also `environment` in this file's frontmatter):

```bash
curl -fsSL https://unitycatalog.io/docs/env/unitycatalog.tar.gz | tar -xz
cd uc-docs-env/unitycatalog && docker compose up -d --wait
export UNITY_CATALOG_URL=http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog
```

- [`delta_api_semantics.py`](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/delta-api/snippets/delta_api_semantics.py) (Python): How the Unity Catalog Delta API behaves on the wire, with plain HTTP. It is
  - run: `UNITY_CATALOG_URL=http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog uv run https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/delta-api/snippets/delta_api_semantics.py`

The *Delta API* is a versioned REST interface that [Unity Catalog](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/what-is-unity-catalog/ "The open-source reference server implementing the Unity Catalog specification.") serves under `/api/2.1/unity-catalog/delta/v1/`, next to the Unity Catalog REST API's `/tables` endpoints. A [Delta](https://delta.io "Open table-format specification: ACID transactions, schema evolution, and time travel over object storage.") client uses it to stage, create, load, and commit to a catalog-managed Delta table. [External tables and catalog-managed Delta tables](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/external-and-managed-tables/) walks through that lifecycle. This page explains why each part of the API is designed the way it is.

The diagram follows one table through the API, from negotiation to its first commit. Expand it to step through each call:

A query engine negotiates with GET /delta/v1/config, stages a table and gets back its location, a READ\_WRITE credential, and the required protocol, writes version 0 to object storage, creates the table, then loads it, writes a staged commit, and posts that commit with assert-table-uuid and assert-etag before publishing it to the Delta log

```mermaid
---
title: "UC Delta API"
---
sequenceDiagram
  participant lakehouse_queryEngine as Query engine
  participant unityCatalogSpec as Unity Catalog
  participant lakehouse_objectStorage as Object storage
  lakehouse_queryEngine->>unityCatalogSpec: GET /delta/v1/config (negotiate endpoints + protocol-version)
  lakehouse_queryEngine->>unityCatalogSpec: POST .../staging-tables { name }
  unityCatalogSpec-->>lakehouse_queryEngine: table-id, location, READ_WRITE credential, required-protocol
  lakehouse_queryEngine->>lakehouse_objectStorage: write _delta_log/0.json (schema, protocol, io.unitycatalog.tableId)
  lakehouse_queryEngine->>unityCatalogSpec: POST .../tables (promote: columns, protocol, properties)
  unityCatalogSpec-->>lakehouse_queryEngine: loadTable response (table-uuid, etag, version 0)
  lakehouse_queryEngine->>unityCatalogSpec: GET .../tables/{table} (loadTable: current etag + uuid)
  lakehouse_queryEngine->>lakehouse_objectStorage: write _delta_log/_staged_commits/<v>.<uuid>.json
  lakehouse_queryEngine->>unityCatalogSpec: POST .../tables/{table} { requirements: [assert-table-uuid, assert-etag], updates: [add-commit] }
  unityCatalogSpec-->>lakehouse_queryEngine: ratified — loadTable with the new commit
  lakehouse_queryEngine->>lakehouse_objectStorage: publish _delta_log/<v>.json (vended credential)
```

This page's script, `delta_api_semantics.py`, sends the requests shown here to a server and checks the responses the page describes.

## One endpoint takes requirements and updates

A commit proposal and every metadata change to a table go to one endpoint, `POST …/tables/{table}`, as a list of preconditions (`requirements`) and a list of intents (`updates`). Dropping and renaming a table have endpoints of their own. The server checks every requirement, then applies every update, or applies none. A request that sets a comment and a property looks like this:

`update-request.json`

```json
{
  "requirements": [
    { "type": "assert-table-uuid", "uuid": "<table-uuid>" },
    { "type": "assert-etag", "etag": "<etag>" }
  ],
  "updates": [
    { "action": "set-table-comment", "comment": "One row per order" },
    { "action": "set-properties", "updates": { "sales.owner": "orders-team" } }
  ]
}
```

The same envelope carries a new commit (`add-commit`), a schema change, a protocol upgrade, and a property change. They can share one request, so a change and the commit that writes it land together or not at all.

All or nothing extends to a request the server rejects as malformed. A request may carry at most one update of each action type, `add-commit` included, and at most one requirement of each type ([spec](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/blob/v0.7.0/spec/protocols/ManagedDeltaTablesSpec.md#write-a-commit), [`delta.yaml`](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/blob/v0.7.0/api/delta.yaml)). The file actions a writer repeats, Delta's `add` and `remove`, aren't actions in this API. They live in the commit file that the one `add-commit` names, and a commit file holds as many as the commit needs. A `set-properties` and a `remove-properties` that touch the same key are rejected rather than applied in order. The order of entries in either list carries no meaning, because the server applies actions in a fixed order of its own ([spec](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/blob/v0.7.0/spec/protocols/ManagedDeltaTablesSpec.md#write-a-commit)). When the server rejects one, none of its valid updates apply either, and the table's etag stays the same.

## Negotiation comes first

Before any other request, a client asks `GET /delta/v1/config` with a `catalog` and the `protocol-versions` it supports. Both parameters are required, and a missing one is a 400. The answer names a protocol version and the endpoints the server offers for it:

`config-response.json (condensed)`

```json
{
  "endpoints": [
    "POST /v1/catalogs/warehouse/schemas/{schema}/staging-tables",
    "GET /v1/catalogs/warehouse/schemas/{schema}/tables/{table}",
    "POST /v1/catalogs/warehouse/schemas/{schema}/tables/{table}",
    "GET /v1/staging-tables/{table_id}/credentials"
  ],
  "protocol-version": "1.0"
}
```

The endpoints come back as strings, and clients route by them instead of building paths. The strings carry the resolved catalog name, `warehouse` here, while the schema and table segments stay templates. That design leaves room to change the API:

- The version lives in each returned path (`/v1/…`), so a later protocol version can lay out its paths however it needs.
- A server may list endpoints beyond the specification's. Clients ignore strings they don't recognize, so a new endpoint doesn't break an old client.
- The [specification](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/blob/v0.7.0/spec/protocols/ManagedDeltaTablesSpec.md#get-configuration) treats a 404 on `config` as a server that doesn't support the protocol, and tells the client to fall back to the Unity Catalog table APIs. An unknown catalog is also a 404. Its error type, `NoSuchCatalogException`, tells the two apart.

The specification defines a negotiation: the client offers the highest version it supports per major version, and the server picks the highest version both support. The Unity Catalog server doesn't negotiate. It ignores `protocol-versions` and answers `1.0` whatever the client offers, even `2.0` alone. Check that the returned `protocol-version` is one you offered. Treat any other answer as an unsupported server, as the specification does for a 400.

`config` covers the protocol version and its endpoints, not table features. The catalog states those when a table is staged.

## The catalog sets table features at staging

When a client stages a table, the catalog states the Delta protocol the table must use: a required protocol and properties, and a suggested protocol and properties. Condensed, the server's answer reads:

`staging-response.json (condensed)`

```json
{
  "table-id": "<table-id>",
  "location": "<location>",
  "storage-credentials": [
    { "prefix": "<location>", "operation": "READ_WRITE" }
  ],
  "required-protocol": {
    "min-reader-version": 3,
    "min-writer-version": 7,
    "reader-features": ["catalogManaged", "v2Checkpoint", "vacuumProtocolCheck", "deletionVectors"],
    "writer-features": ["catalogManaged", "v2Checkpoint", "vacuumProtocolCheck", "deletionVectors", "inCommitTimestamp"]
  },
  "suggested-protocol": {
    "reader-features": ["columnMapping"],
    "writer-features": ["columnMapping", "domainMetadata", "rowTracking"]
  },
  "required-properties": {
    "delta.enableInCommitTimestamps": "true",
    "io.unitycatalog.tableId": "<table-id>"
  },
  "suggested-properties": {
    "delta.columnMapping.mode": "name",
    "delta.columnMapping.maxColumnId": null
  }
}
```

The required protocol is reader version 3 and writer version 7. Its reader and writer features are `catalogManaged`, `v2Checkpoint`, `vacuumProtocolCheck`, and `deletionVectors`, and the writer features add `inCommitTimestamp`. The required properties include `io.unitycatalog.tableId`, which equals the staging table's ID.

A `null` value means the engine generates the value. The catalog asks for column mapping in `name` mode but leaves `delta.columnMapping.maxColumnId` to the engine that assigns the column IDs. The catalog names the property, and the engine, which knows the schema, fills it in.

The response is authoritative. The specification's [list of features](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/blob/v0.7.0/spec/protocols/ManagedDeltaTablesSpec.md#reference-table-features-and-properties-for-unity-catalog-managed-tables) is a non-normative reference, and the specification lets a catalog grow or shrink the set. Clients read the response fields rather than hard-coding a list. A catalog that serves a stateful compaction service, for example, may require `domainMetadata` so that the service's state is kept with the table. Unity Catalog OSS ships a fixed set, defined in [`UcManagedDeltaContract.java`](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/blob/v0.7.0/server/src/main/java/io/unitycatalog/server/service/delta/UcManagedDeltaContract.java). When the client then creates the table, the server checks the declared protocol and properties against the managed-table contract.

The staging response also carries one `READ_WRITE` credential whose prefix is the table's location, so the engine can write version 0 without standing access to the bucket. [Credential vending](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/credential-vending/) explains that trust boundary.

## Optimistic concurrency with assert-table-uuid and assert-etag

The API doesn't lock tables. A writer loads the table, prepares its change, and states in `requirements` what it assumed when it loaded:

- **`assert-table-uuid`** is required on every request. A request without it is a 400 (`assert-table-uuid requirement is required`). Names get reused: a table can be dropped and created again under the same name. UUIDs don't, so the assertion stops a change meant for the old table from landing on the new one.
- **`assert-etag`** is optional. The etag is an opaque token from `loadTable`. If the table has changed since, the server answers 409 `UpdateRequirementConflictException` and applies nothing:

  `conflict-response.json`

  ```json
  {
    "error": {
      "type": "UpdateRequirementConflictException",
      "code": 409,
      "message": "<assert-etag failed: expected … but table has …>"
    }
  }
  ```

An `add-commit` for version `v` also asserts, without saying so, that the table is at version `v-1`. Commits go in order, one version at a time: after a Spark `INSERT`, the table's latest version is one higher, and its newest commit carries that version. When another writer has already taken the version, the [specification](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/blob/v0.7.0/spec/protocols/ManagedDeltaTablesSpec.md#write-a-commit) defines a second 409, `CommitVersionConflictException`. So a 409 comes in two kinds: the version was taken, or a requirement failed. Either way, the change didn't land.

### Retry or rebase

The two kinds of failure call for different responses. The specification's [commit recovery](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/blob/v0.7.0/spec/protocols/ManagedDeltaTablesSpec.md#commit-recovery) rules say:

- **On a 5xx or a timeout, resend the identical request.** The outcome is unknown, and the server deduplicates a retry by the staged commit's file name. A byte-for-byte retry resolves to what happened the first time.
- **Rebase only once you know the attempt didn't land.** A 409 tells you, and so does a reload that shows another writer's commit at the proposed version. Rebasing means building the commit again against the reloaded state, with a new commit file. Rebasing while the outcome is unknown can commit the same change twice.
- **Abort if the reloaded UUID differs.** The table was dropped and created again under the same name, so the change no longer has a target.

## Metadata changes travel with add-commit

A catalog-managed table has two views of its metadata: the catalog's record and the Delta log. The API keeps them in lockstep with one rule. A change that the Delta log also represents, such as the schema, the protocol, or a `delta.*` property, goes in the same request as the `add-commit` whose commit file writes it. A change that lives only in the catalog, such as the table comment, may go alone. Engines follow the rule: after a Spark `ALTER TABLE … ADD COLUMNS`, the table's version is one higher, and both the Delta API and the Unity Catalog REST API list the new column.

The rule falls on the client. The specification doesn't require the server to inspect staged commit files ([spec](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/blob/v0.7.0/spec/protocols/ManagedDeltaTablesSpec.md#catalog-and-log-consistency)), so clients can't rely on it to check that declared metadata matches the commit file, and they own the consistency of the two views. If the two views diverge anyway, the Delta log wins for snapshots: engines rebuild the table from its commits, and the catalog's record serves discovery.

> **Warning**
>
> The server accepts a log-represented change with no commit. A `set-properties` that turns `delta.enableDeletionVectors` off on a managed table succeeds without a new version, and the Delta log keeps the old value. The specification calls such a request a client error. Don't rely on the server to catch it: send log-represented changes only with the `add-commit` that writes them.

An external table has no `add-commit`, because the catalog doesn't accept its commits. Its sync is metadata-only: the client sends what it reads from the Delta log to the catalog's record, as in [Sync the catalog's record](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/change-table-schema/#sync-the-catalogs-record).

## Delta's own schema on the wire

The Delta API sends a table's columns as a Delta struct type, the same shape as `metaData.schemaString` in the Delta log. Column-mapping metadata travels with each field:

`columns-response.json (one field)`

```json
{
  "metadata": {
    "columns": {
      "type": "struct",
      "fields": [
        {
          "name": "order_id",
          "type": "long",
          "nullable": true,
          "metadata": {
            "delta.columnMapping.id": 1,
            "delta.columnMapping.physicalName": "<physical-name>"
          }
        }
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

The protocol travels the same way, as reader and writer features. Nothing is translated: an engine gets the schema in the shape it writes to the log, with the column IDs and physical names it assigned.

Compare the Unity Catalog REST API, which describes each column as a `ColumnInfo` with `type_name`, `type_text`, and `type_json`. That shape serves every format the catalog registers. The Delta API serves only Delta tables, so it uses Delta's own shapes.

## Further reading

- [External tables and catalog-managed Delta tables](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/external-and-managed-tables/) walks through the lifecycle of a catalog-managed table.
- [Credential vending](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/credential-vending/) explains the credentials the staging and table responses carry.
- [Manage schemas and properties](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/change-table-schema/) uses the Delta API to sync an external table's record.
- The [managed Delta tables specification](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/blob/v0.7.0/spec/protocols/ManagedDeltaTablesSpec.md) defines the protocol, and the [Delta API definition](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/blob/v0.7.0/api/delta.yaml) defines every endpoint and field.
- The [Delta protocol](https://github.com/delta-io/delta/blob/v4.3.1/PROTOCOL.md#catalog-managed-tables) defines catalog-managed tables from the table's side.

---

# https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/uc-basics/

Unity Catalog is a registry of named objects. Each object has an owner and a set of grants that decide who can use it, and most objects describe files that live somewhere else. The umbrella term for these objects is *securable*.

This page follows the order in which a catalog is built up:

1. the **namespace** that names every asset;
2. **catalog administration**: the metastore, catalogs, and schemas, and the credentials and external locations that let the server reach storage;
3. the **data and AI assets** that users, pipelines, and agents work with;
4. how those objects relate to the **files** they describe;
5. the **privileges** the server checks on each object;
6. the **users** those privileges are granted to.

## The three-level namespace

Assets are addressed by a three-part name, `catalog.schema.object`:

```text
metastore
├── catalog                     retail
│   └── schema                  retail.sales
│       ├── table / view        retail.sales.orders
│       ├── volume              retail.sales.landing
│       ├── function            retail.sales.normalize_sku
│       └── registered model    retail.sales.churn
│           └── model version   retail.sales.churn, version 3
├── storage credential          acme-lake-role
└── external location           acme-lake-retail
```

Names are unique within their parent: two schemas may both contain an `orders` table, but their full names differ. Clients refer to assets by full name and never need to know where the files are. Storage credentials and external locations sit outside the namespace. They have single-part names and are addressed by name alone.

## Catalog administration

### Metastore, catalogs, and schemas

The **metastore** is the top-level container. An open source server has exactly one. It has an ID (`GET /metastore_summary`) but no name, and it never appears in object names. Privileges that aren't tied to a catalog, such as creating catalogs, are granted on the metastore.

A **catalog** is the first level of the namespace. Teams typically use catalogs to separate business units, environments, or data products. A **schema** sits inside one catalog and groups related assets. Every asset belongs to exactly one schema.

### External data access

Two kinds of object live directly under the metastore and hold no data. They decide which storage the server can reach, and on whose behalf.

- A **storage credential** holds the cloud identity the server uses to reach storage. In this release every credential has the purpose `STORAGE`, and the credential service implements AWS IAM roles. Azure and Google Cloud access are configured on the server rather than as credential objects.
- An **external location** pairs a storage path, such as `s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/retail/`, with a storage credential. It doesn't have to be a bucket root. A location can cover any path prefix, and narrower locations give narrower control. External locations decide who may create external tables and volumes under a path, use it as managed storage, or read and write its files directly.

With these objects in place, the server can hand out short-lived credentials scoped to a single asset or path. It exposes one endpoint each for tables, volumes, model versions, and raw paths. See [Credential vending](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/credential-vending/).

### Managed storage roots

The metastore, a catalog, and a schema can each declare a `storage_root`. When the server creates a managed object, it takes the location from the nearest root:

1. the schema's `storage_root`, if it has one;
2. otherwise the catalog's `storage_root`;
3. otherwise the metastore's `storage_root`.

The server allocates a unique path below that root, under a reserved `__unitystorage` prefix, for example `<root>/__unitystorage/schemas/<schema id>/volumes/<volume id>`. External objects may not use paths containing `__unitystorage`.

## Data and AI assets

Every asset lives in a schema. The *securable type* is the name the permissions API uses for the object.

| Object           | Securable type     | What it describes                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| ---------------- | ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Table            | `table`            | Tabular data with a column schema and a format, such as Delta or Parquet. Its *table type* says who manages it: `EXTERNAL` or `MANAGED`. SQL views (`VIEW`) and metric views (`METRIC_VIEW`) are stored as table types too, with a definition instead of a storage location. |
| Volume           | `volume`           | A directory of non-tabular files, either `EXTERNAL` or `MANAGED`.                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| Function         | `function`         | A registered routine with typed parameters and a body. The catalog stores the definition, and the caller's environment runs it.                                                                                                                                              |
| Registered model | `registered_model` | A named ML model with numbered *model versions*. Each version has its own storage location for its artifacts. Versions aren't securables of their own: privileges on the model cover them.                                                                                   |

A managed Delta table starts life as a *staging table*: the server reserves a location, the client writes the first commit there, and creating the table ratifies it. See [External tables and catalog-managed Delta tables](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/external-and-managed-tables/).

A view holds no data. The catalog stores its definition, and the engine that queries it runs that definition. See [SQL views and metric views as catalog objects](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/views-and-metric-views/).

The API's `TableType` enum also lists `STREAMING_TABLE` and `MATERIALIZED_VIEW`. An enum value is not the same as a supported workflow, so check the release's compatibility notes before relying on those types.

## Objects versus files

A catalog object and the files it describes are separate things. Unity Catalog stores names, columns, comments, and a location. The files sit in object storage or on a local disk. Three consequences follow.

**Renaming moves nothing.** Renaming a schema or a volume changes its catalog name only. The files stay at the same location, and clients that look the object up by name find it under the new name.

**External and managed decide who owns the files.** For an *external* table or volume, you supply the location and keep control of its lifecycle. Dropping the object deletes only the catalog entry. For a *managed* table or volume, the server allocates the location below a storage root and treats the files as part of the object. Dropping it deletes them too, once a cleanup delay passes (7 days by default).

**One file, one object.** An external table or volume may not overlap another one's location, so any one file is governed by a single object.

The catalog doesn't stand between a client and storage. A client that can reach the files directly, through its own cloud credentials or a shared disk, can read them without asking Unity Catalog. To make the catalog the gatekeeper, withhold direct storage access and have clients request temporary, scoped credentials from the server.

## Ownership and privileges

The server checks privileges only when authorization is enabled (`server.authorization=enable` in `server.properties`). With it disabled, every request is allowed.

Every securable has an owner. The principal that creates an object becomes its owner. `OWNER` is the only privilege that implies the others: the owner can read, modify, drop, and grant privileges on the object. The server has no `ALL PRIVILEGES`, `MANAGE`, or `BROWSE`. The server's checks honor ownership on the way down: the owner of a catalog can manage every schema and asset in it, and the owner of a schema can manage every asset in that schema. The metastore owner is the server's administrator.

Other principals need privileges. The server checks each privilege on a specific object type:

| Checked on                 | Privileges                                                                                               |
| -------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Metastore                  | `CREATE CATALOG`, `CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION`, `CREATE STORAGE CREDENTIAL`                                |
| Catalog                    | `USE CATALOG`, `CREATE SCHEMA`                                                                           |
| Schema                     | `USE SCHEMA`, `CREATE TABLE`, `CREATE VOLUME`, `CREATE FUNCTION`, `CREATE MODEL`                         |
| Table                      | `SELECT`, `MODIFY`                                                                                       |
| Volume                     | `READ VOLUME`                                                                                            |
| Function, registered model | `EXECUTE`                                                                                                |
| Storage credential         | `CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION`                                                                               |
| External location          | `CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE`, `CREATE EXTERNAL VOLUME`, `CREATE MANAGED STORAGE`, `READ FILES`, `WRITE FILES` |

Access to an asset also needs access to its parents. Reading a table takes `SELECT` on the table, `USE SCHEMA` on its schema, and `USE CATALOG` on its catalog. Writing to it takes both `SELECT` and `MODIFY`. `USE CATALOG` and `USE SCHEMA` don't grant access to anything inside on their own. They let a principal reach the objects it holds other privileges on. Creating an object works the same way: a `CREATE …` privilege on the parent, plus `USE` on every level above it.

Privileges other than `OWNER` are inherited. A privilege granted on a catalog or schema also applies to every object below it, so `SELECT` on a schema covers every table in it, including tables created later. `OWNER` applies only to the object it's held on.

Grants are read and changed through the permissions API, which addresses an object by its securable type and full name (`/permissions/{securable_type}/{full_name}`). A change adds or removes privileges for one principal. The CLI wraps the same calls in `bin/uc permission create | get | delete`.

The how-to guides list the privileges each operation needs, for example [Manage catalogs and schemas](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/manage-catalogs-and-schemas/) and [Manage volumes](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/manage-volumes/).

## Principals and users

A principal in the open source server is a user, identified by email address. The server has no groups or service principals, so every grant names an individual user.

The server keeps its own user list, managed through a SCIM 2.0 Users API under `/api/1.0/unity-control/scim2/Users` (create, list, get, update, delete) and `/scim2/Me` for the calling user. The CLI wraps it as `bin/uc user`. A user record holds a display name, an email address, an optional external ID, and an active flag.

Users authenticate with an identity provider, such as Google, then exchange that provider's token for a Unity Catalog token at `/auth/tokens`. The exchange succeeds only for an active user that is already registered on the server. Registration and grants are two separate steps: a new user can sign in but reaches nothing until someone grants them privileges.

On first start with authorization enabled, the server creates an `admin` user, makes it the metastore owner, and writes a token for it to `etc/conf/token.txt`. That account is the bootstrap: use it to register the first real users and grant them access.

> **Note**
>
> This page describes the open source server's behavior, based on its API definitions and authorization source. Databricks Unity Catalog adds securables and governance features beyond it, so a Databricks guide may not apply here.

---

# https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/external-and-managed-tables/

Unity Catalog knows two kinds of table. They differ in two things: who owns the files, and who decides which version of the table is the current one. This page explains both kinds, what the server does for a catalog-managed [Delta](https://delta.io "Open table-format specification: ACID transactions, schema evolution, and time travel over object storage.") table, and which engines can use each kind.

## Two questions decide the kind

**Who owns the files?** An *external* table points at a location that someone else chose and controls. The catalog records the table's name, columns, format, and location, and never moves or deletes the files. A *managed* table lives at a location the catalog chooses, under the storage root of its schema or catalog. The catalog creates that location, and deletes it when the table is dropped.

**Who decides the latest version?** A Delta table is a series of numbered commits in its `_delta_log`. For an external table, the files decide: whichever writer manages to put commit file `N` in place first has made version `N`, and the catalog plays no part. For a *catalog-managed* Delta table, the catalog decides. A writer proposes commit `N`, and it becomes the table's version `N` only once the server accepts it.

In Unity Catalog the two answers go together. Managed tables are always Delta, and a client that creates one through the Delta API, such as Spark with Delta 4.3 or later, makes it catalog-managed. External tables never are.

|                     | External table                                                              | Managed (catalog-managed Delta) table                                                            |
| ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Location            | You supply it                                                               | The catalog allocates it                                                                         |
| Who accepts commits | The files, first writer wins                                                | The Unity Catalog server                                                                         |
| Formats             | Delta, Parquet, CSV, and others                                             | Delta only                                                                                       |
| Dropping the table  | Removes the catalog entry, keeps the files                                  | Deletes the files too, after a cleanup delay                                                     |
| Path-based clients  | Can read and write the location                                             | Can't load it without the catalog                                                                |
| How to create one   | [Register it](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/register-external-table/) | [`CREATE TABLE` without a location](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/tutorials/managed-delta-table/) |

## Why a catalog should accept commits

When the files decide, the storage system has to resolve races between writers, and every guarantee follows from that one atomic file operation. That has worked for years, but it leaves the catalog as a bystander. The catalog can't reject a commit that breaks a rule, can't see a commit before it lands, and can't coordinate changes across tables.

When the catalog accepts commits, it becomes the table's source of truth. Two writers that race for the same version get one acceptance and one rejection, whatever the storage system offers. The catalog can require table features, such as deletion vectors or in-commit timestamps, before a table may exist. A reader asks the catalog for the latest version instead of listing files.

Delta records this arrangement in the table itself as the `catalogManaged` table feature. The [Delta protocol](https://github.com/delta-io/delta/blob/v4.3.1/PROTOCOL.md#catalog-managed-tables) requires every client that reads or writes such a table to ask the catalog.

## The lifecycle through the Delta API

The server speaks to Delta clients through the *Delta API*, a versioned REST interface under `/api/2.1/unity-catalog/delta/v1/`. Its [managed-tables protocol](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/blob/v0.7.0/spec/protocols/ManagedDeltaTablesSpec.md) defines each step. Expand the diagram and step through it:

The managed-table lifecycle through the Delta API

```mermaid
---
title: "UC Delta API"
---
sequenceDiagram
  participant lakehouse_queryEngine as Query engine
  participant unityCatalogSpec as Unity Catalog
  participant lakehouse_objectStorage as Object storage
  lakehouse_queryEngine->>unityCatalogSpec: GET /delta/v1/config (negotiate endpoints + protocol-version)
  lakehouse_queryEngine->>unityCatalogSpec: POST .../staging-tables { name }
  unityCatalogSpec-->>lakehouse_queryEngine: table-id, location, READ_WRITE credential, required-protocol
  lakehouse_queryEngine->>lakehouse_objectStorage: write _delta_log/0.json (schema, protocol, io.unitycatalog.tableId)
  lakehouse_queryEngine->>unityCatalogSpec: POST .../tables (promote: columns, protocol, properties)
  unityCatalogSpec-->>lakehouse_queryEngine: loadTable response (table-uuid, etag, version 0)
  lakehouse_queryEngine->>unityCatalogSpec: GET .../tables/{table} (loadTable: current etag + uuid)
  lakehouse_queryEngine->>lakehouse_objectStorage: write _delta_log/_staged_commits/<v>.<uuid>.json
  lakehouse_queryEngine->>unityCatalogSpec: POST .../tables/{table} { requirements: [assert-table-uuid, assert-etag], updates: [add-commit] }
  unityCatalogSpec-->>lakehouse_queryEngine: ratified — loadTable with the new commit
  lakehouse_queryEngine->>lakehouse_objectStorage: publish _delta_log/<v>.json (vended credential)
```

The lifecycle has four parts.

1. **Negotiate.** The client asks `GET /delta/v1/config` which endpoints and which protocol version the server supports. The server answers with the endpoints it implements and protocol version `1.0`.
2. **Stage.** To create a table, the client asks for a *staging table*. The server picks the location, issues a read-write credential for it, and states the Delta protocol the table must use. The server answers like this:

   ```json
   {
     "table-type": "MANAGED",
     "location": "file:///tmp/uc-docs/managed/__unitystorage/catalogs/<catalog-id>/tables/<table-id>",
     "required-protocol": {
       "min-reader-version": 3,
       "min-writer-version": 7,
       "reader-features": ["catalogManaged", "v2Checkpoint", "vacuumProtocolCheck", "deletionVectors"],
       "writer-features": ["catalogManaged", "v2Checkpoint", "vacuumProtocolCheck", "deletionVectors", "inCommitTimestamp"]
     },
     "suggested-protocol": {
       "reader-features": ["columnMapping"],
       "writer-features": ["columnMapping", "domainMetadata", "rowTracking"]
     }
   }
   ```

   The response also lists the matching required and suggested table properties. The client writes version 0 of the Delta log at that location, then asks the server to turn the staging table into a real one.
3. **Commit.** For each change, the client writes the new data files and a commit file under `_delta_log/_staged_commits/`, named with the version and a random ID. It then sends one request that names the commit and the conditions under which to accept it, for example that the table is still the one it loaded. The server checks the conditions and accepts or rejects the commit as a whole.
4. **Load.** A reader asks the server for the table. The response includes the latest accepted version and the recent commits, so the reader knows exactly which files make up the table.

Throughout, the server hands out storage credentials scoped to the table's location, so no client needs standing access to the whole bucket. See [Credential vending](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/credential-vending/) for that trust boundary.

## What clients must support

Because the protocol lives in the table, a client that doesn't speak it can't use the table at all, not even to read it. Unity Catalog gives a path-based client nothing to work with: delta-rs 1.6.6, pointed at a managed table's location, stops with `Max catalog version is required when loading a catalog-managed table`. That refusal is deliberate. A client that only lists files could miss commits the catalog has accepted, or write a version the catalog never approved.

So for a managed table, choose a client that goes through the catalog. These include Spark with the Unity Catalog connector and Delta 4.3 or later, and DuckDB's `unity_catalog` extension for reads and appends.

An external table makes the opposite trade. Any client with access to the storage can read and write it, including tools that have never heard of Unity Catalog. That suits data that another system already owns. But the catalog can't coordinate those writers, and its record of the columns can fall out of step with the files.

What each client can do with a table, as tested in CI:

| Operation                                  | [Spark 4.1](https://spark.apache.org "Unified analytics engine for large-scale data processing.")                                                   | [DuckDB](https://duckdb.org "In-process analytical SQL engine.")                                                | [Polars](https://pola.rs "Fast DataFrame library written in Rust, with a Python API.")                          | [Daft](https://docs.daft.ai/en/stable/connectors/unity_catalog/ "Distributed Python DataFrame library with a Unity Catalog integration.") | [pandas](https://delta-io.github.io/delta-rs/ "Native Rust implementation of the Delta protocol with Python bindings.") | [PyIceberg](https://py.iceberg.apache.org "Python implementation of Apache Iceberg with REST catalog and table APIs.") | [DataFusion · Rust](https://datafusion.apache.org "Extensible, high-performance query engine in Rust using Apache Arrow.") | [uc CLI 0.7](https://docs.unitycatalog.io/how-to/run-local-server#run-the-uc-cli "Command-line client for managing Unity Catalog objects and storage access.") | [Python SDK 0.7](https://pypi.org/project/unitycatalog-client/ "Generated asynchronous Python client for Unity Catalog REST APIs.") |
| ------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| List tables                                | [✓](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/configure-spark/#check-the-connection)                                                                      | [✓](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/duckdb/#list-tables)                                                    | [✓](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/python-dataframes/#list-tables)                                         | [✓](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/python-dataframes/#list-tables)                                                                   | ✗                                                                                                                       | —                                                                                                                      | —                                                                                                                          | [✓](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/tutorials/getting-started/#browse-the-sample-data)                                                                            | —                                                                                                                                   |
| Read an external table                     | —                                                                                                                                                   | [✓](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/register-external-table/#read-the-data)                                 | [✓](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/register-external-table/#read-the-data)                                 | [✓](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/register-external-table/#read-the-data)                                                           | [✓](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/python-dataframes/#read-a-table)                                                | —                                                                                                                      | —                                                                                                                          | —                                                                                                                                                              | —                                                                                                                                   |

## When to use which

Use a managed table when Unity Catalog should own the data. You get a location nobody has to plan, commits that the catalog checks, and clean deletion.

Use an external table when the data already exists, when another system writes it, or when it isn't in Delta format. Registering such a table gives it a governed name without changing who writes it.

## Further reading

- [Create and update a catalog-managed Delta table](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/tutorials/managed-delta-table/) walks the lifecycle above with Spark.
- [Core concepts](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/uc-basics/) explains storage roots and how managed locations are inherited.
- The [Delta API specification](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/blob/v0.7.0/api/delta.yaml) defines every endpoint and field.

---

# https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/credential-vending/

Engines read and write a lakehouse's data directly in object storage, so something has to give them access to that storage. With *credential vending*, the [Unity Catalog](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/what-is-unity-catalog/ "The open-source reference server implementing the Unity Catalog specification.") server gives it. The server holds the one identity that can reach the storage. A client proves who it is to the catalog and asks for access to a single table, volume, model version, or path. If the catalog's grants allow it, the server returns a credential that works only for that location and that kind of access, and that expires within an hour. This page explains how that exchange works and where its guarantees end.

## Why vend credentials instead of sharing keys

The alternative is to give every engine and user a storage key, or to keep a bucket policy for each of them. Each key is a standing secret that can leak. It usually reaches far more data than its holder needs. Revoking access means rotating the key everywhere it was copied, and the catalog's grants and the storage's permissions drift apart.

Vending moves the long-lived secret into one place, the catalog server, and gives clients only short-lived, narrow credentials. That has three effects:

- **Clients prove identity and never hold long-lived keys.** A client authenticates to the catalog with its own token. The storage identity never leaves the server.
- **Each credential has a small blast radius.** It covers one location and one operation, so a leaked credential exposes one table's files for at most an hour.
- **Grants take effect quickly.** Every credential request passes the catalog's authorization check. Revoke a grant and the next request fails. The longest delay is the remaining lifetime of a credential already handed out. No key needs rotating.

The catalog makes the access decision, and the storage enforces it on every request. Neither has to trust the client.

## The flow

A client that reads a table makes two calls to the catalog before it touches storage. Expand the diagram and step through it:

Credential vending for a table read: the engine resolves the table, asks Unity Catalog for a credential, the server authorizes and mints a scoped credential through the storage credential issuer, and the engine reads object storage with it

```mermaid
---
title: "UC credential vending"
---
sequenceDiagram
  participant lakehouse_queryEngine as Query engine
  participant unityCatalogServer as Unity Catalog (OSS)
  participant lakehouse_credentialIssuer as Storage credential issuer
  participant lakehouse_objectStorage as Object storage
  lakehouse_queryEngine->>unityCatalogServer: GET /tables/{full_name} (bearer token)
  lakehouse_queryEngine->>unityCatalogServer: POST /temporary-table-credentials { table_id, operation: READ }
  unityCatalogServer->>unityCatalogServer: authorize: USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA, SELECT
  unityCatalogServer->>lakehouse_credentialIssuer: mint a credential for the table's location
  lakehouse_credentialIssuer-->>unityCatalogServer: short-lived, scoped credential
  unityCatalogServer-->>lakehouse_queryEngine: temporary credentials, expiration_time, url
  lakehouse_queryEngine->>lakehouse_objectStorage: read files under the location
  lakehouse_objectStorage-->>lakehouse_queryEngine: data, or AccessDenied outside the scope
  lakehouse_queryEngine->>unityCatalogServer: renew before expiration_time
```

1. **Resolve.** The client looks up the table by name with its own bearer token. The answer includes the table's ID and its storage location.
2. **Request.** The client asks `POST /temporary-table-credentials` for that table ID and an operation, `READ` or `READ_WRITE`.
3. **Authorize.** The server checks the caller's privileges. A read needs `USE CATALOG`, `USE SCHEMA`, and `SELECT` on the table. A write also needs `MODIFY`. Ownership covers both. If the check fails, no credential is minted.
4. **Mint.** The server finds the external location that contains the table's path and uses that location's storage credential. It asks the cloud's credential issuer for a credential narrowed to the table's location and the requested operation.
5. **Return.** The client receives the credential, the URL it covers, and an `expiration_time` in epoch milliseconds.
6. **Read.** The client reads the files straight from storage. Data never flows through the catalog. The storage rejects any request outside the credential's scope.
7. **Renew.** Before the credential expires, a long-running client asks again, and the server checks the grants again.

Volumes, model versions, and paths follow the same flow through their own endpoints.

## What a credential covers

The server vends credentials through four endpoints. Each request names one object and one operation, and the privileges it needs depend on both. A request for anything inside a schema also needs `USE CATALOG` and `USE SCHEMA` on its parents, or ownership of them.

| Endpoint                               | Operations                                          | Privileges required                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| -------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `/temporary-table-credentials`         | `READ`, `READ_WRITE`                                | `SELECT` to read; `SELECT` and `MODIFY` to write; or ownership                                                                                                                                                              |
| `/temporary-volume-credentials`        | `READ_VOLUME`, `WRITE_VOLUME`                       | `READ VOLUME` to read; ownership to write                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| `/temporary-model-version-credentials` | `READ_MODEL_VERSION`, `READ_WRITE_MODEL_VERSION`    | `EXECUTE` on the registered model to read; ownership to write                                                                                                                                                               |
| `/temporary-path-credentials`          | `PATH_READ`, `PATH_READ_WRITE`, `PATH_CREATE_TABLE` | The privileges of the object that owns the path. For a path no object owns: `READ FILES` on the external location to read, `READ FILES` and `WRITE FILES` to write, `CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE` to create a table, or ownership |

A path request can't get around a table's grants. If the path falls inside a table or volume, the server applies that object's privileges, as if the client had asked for the object itself.

Engines that speak the [Delta API](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/external-and-managed-tables/) get credentials from its own endpoints, with the same checks. When a client creates a catalog-managed table, the staging response already includes a read-write credential for the new table's location. The [Iceberg REST API](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/iceberg-rest/) returns a credential with each table it loads, plus the endpoint the client calls to renew it before it expires.

## How the server mints a credential

The server never stores credentials for individual tables. It works them out when asked. The table's storage location falls under exactly one *external location*, which names a *storage credential*, which holds the identity the server uses with the cloud. External locations can't overlap, so the answer is always unique. See [Core concepts](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/uc-basics/) for how locations and storage roots fit together.

Each cloud narrows the credential differently:

| Storage                 | How the credential is narrowed                                                                                                        | What the client receives                                      |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Amazon S3               | The server calls AWS STS `AssumeRole` on the storage role, with a session policy that allows only the requested prefix and operation. | Access key, secret key, and session token, valid for one hour |
| Azure Data Lake Storage | The server gets a user-delegation key from the storage account and signs a SAS token for the requested path.                          | A user-delegation SAS, valid for one hour                     |
| Google Cloud Storage    | Google STS downscopes the server's token with a credential access boundary on the requested prefix.                                   | An OAuth token                                                |

Storage credentials as catalog objects exist for AWS only. Azure and GCS vending uses server-wide `adls.*` and `gcs.*` settings in `server.properties`, and so does S3 when no external location covers a bucket. For the AWS setup (master role, storage roles, external IDs), see [Configure AWS storage credentials and external locations](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/configure-aws-storage/).

A `file://` location needs no keys. The server still checks the privileges, but its answer carries only the location. That is why local examples print empty credentials.

## Expiry and renewal

A credential expires on its own. Its response carries `expiration_time` in epoch milliseconds. Clients should cache the credential until shortly before then and request a new one, rather than ask again for every file. The Spark connector does this automatically with its `renewCredential.enabled` option (see [Configure Spark](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/configure-spark/)). If you build your own client, give its storage layer a credential callback that asks the catalog again before expiry. obstore's credential providers, for example, cache a credential until the `expires_at` you return.

The server can't recall a credential it has already issued. Revoking a grant stops new credentials, but an existing one stays valid until it expires.

## Where the trust boundary sits

Vending protects data only if the catalog is the only way to reach it. These are the places where that assumption ends:

- **Standing storage access bypasses the catalog.** Anyone who can reach the bucket with their own IAM role or key never asks the catalog, so its grants don't apply to them. Keep direct access to governed locations limited to the server's identity and to operators.
- **A vended credential is a bearer credential.** Storage doesn't know who it was vended to. Whoever holds it can use it until it expires, so treat it like any other secret in logs and job configuration.
- **Access is all-or-nothing per location.** A credential opens every file under the table's location. The catalog can't use it to hide rows or columns, because the client reads the files itself. Row filters and column masks need an engine you trust to apply them.
- **The decision is only as strong as authentication.** With authorization disabled, the server vends to any caller. Enable authentication and authorization before you point the server at real storage.
- **The server's identity is the crown jewel.** The master role, or the keys in `server.properties`, can reach every governed location. Protect the server host and its configuration accordingly.

## Further reading

- [Configure AWS storage credentials and external locations](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/configure-aws-storage/) sets up vending on S3 and checks a vended credential.
- [Set managed storage for catalogs and schemas on S3](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/managed-storage-s3/) puts managed tables and volumes under an external location.
- [Read files from a volume](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/tutorials/read-volume-files/) requests a volume credential and opens storage with it.
- [External tables and catalog-managed Delta tables](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/external-and-managed-tables/) shows where credentials appear in the Delta API lifecycle.

# https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/models-and-mlflow/

## Companion files

CI-tested scripts that run this page's examples end to end. A script that exits 0 has passed its checks.

They need Unity Catalog 0.7.0 with MLflow, simulated S3, and PostgreSQL running. To start it (also `environment` in this file's frontmatter):

```bash
curl -fsSL https://unitycatalog.io/docs/env/uc-mlflow.tar.gz | tar -xz
cd uc-docs-env/uc-mlflow && docker compose up -d --wait
export AWS_ALLOW_HTTP=true
export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:9000
export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3=http://localhost:9000
export AWS_REGION=us-east-1
export MLFLOW_AI_GATEWAY_URL=http://localhost:8080/ai-gateway
export MLFLOW_ENABLE_PROXY_MULTIPART_DOWNLOAD=false
export MLFLOW_ENABLE_PROXY_MULTIPART_UPLOAD=false
export MLFLOW_REGISTRY_URI=uc:http://localhost:8080
export MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI=http://localhost:8080
export UNITY_CATALOG_URL=http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog
```

- [`model_split.py`](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/models-and-mlflow/snippets/model_split.py) (Python): Which service keeps which part of a registered model: MLflow or Unity Catalog.
  - run: `AWS_ALLOW_HTTP=true AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:9000 AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3=http://localhost:9000 AWS_REGION=us-east-1 MLFLOW_AI_GATEWAY_URL=http://localhost:8080/ai-gateway MLFLOW_ENABLE_PROXY_MULTIPART_DOWNLOAD=false MLFLOW_ENABLE_PROXY_MULTIPART_UPLOAD=false MLFLOW_REGISTRY_URI=uc:http://localhost:8080 MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI=http://localhost:8080 UNITY_CATALOG_URL=http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog uv run https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/models-and-mlflow/snippets/model_split.py`

With Unity Catalog as MLflow's registry, a model involves two services. [MLflow](https://mlflow.org "Open source platform for the ML lifecycle: experiment tracking, model registry, and deployment.") records how the model was made. [Unity Catalog](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/what-is-unity-catalog/ "The open-source reference server implementing the Unity Catalog specification.") holds the registered model, such as `unity.model_split.linear`, and its numbered versions. The two services never share a record. A version points back at MLflow by URI, and registering copies the model's files into the catalog's storage. So each side keeps working when the other side's copy is deleted.

## What MLflow tracks

MLflow keeps the training side of the model. An experiment groups runs. A run records its parameters, such as `fit_intercept`, and its metrics, such as `r2`. When the training code calls `log_model`, MLflow creates a *logged model* with a URI of the form `models:/m-<id>`. A logged model has its own identity. It belongs to a run when you log it inside an active run, and otherwise it has no run ([`model.py`](https://github.com/mlflow/mlflow/blob/v3.17.0/mlflow/models/model.py#L1159-L1175)). The logged model holds the files that a later load needs, such as the `MLmodel` descriptor and the serialized model.

All of this lives in MLflow's own stores, not in the catalog. The tracking server writes runs and logged-model metadata to its backend database, and serves the logged model's files from its artifact store through URIs that start with `mlflow-artifacts:/`.

## What Unity Catalog registers

Unity Catalog keeps the governed side of the model: the registered model, its versions, their files, and who may use them.

A registered model lives in a schema next to tables, volumes, and functions, and has a three-level name, `catalog.schema.model`. Each registration adds a version with the next number: 1, 2, 3. A version records its `status`, a `storage_location` for its files, and two links back to MLflow. `source` holds the logged model's URI, `models:/m-<id>`. `run_id` holds the run's ID when you register from a `runs:/<run-id>/<path>` URI, and stays empty when you register from `models:/m-<id>`.

The server chooses a registered model's storage when the model is created. It uses the schema's managed storage, or the catalog's if the schema has none ([`ModelRepository.java`](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/blob/v0.7.0/server/src/main/java/io/unitycatalog/server/persist/ModelRepository.java#L241-L245), [`ExternalLocationUtils.java`](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/blob/v0.7.0/server/src/main/java/io/unitycatalog/server/persist/utils/ExternalLocationUtils.java#L668-L688)). If neither has managed storage, creating the model fails. Each version then gets its own folder under the model's location. In the `uc-mlflow` environment, a version of a model in the `unity` catalog lands at `s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/unity/__unitystorage/catalogs/<id>/models/<id>/versions/<id>`.

A registered model is a securable, so the [privilege model](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/uc-basics/#ownership-and-privileges) applies to it when authorization is enabled. The `uc-mlflow` environment runs with authorization disabled. Creating a model takes `CREATE MODEL` on the schema. Using one takes `EXECUTE` on the model, plus `USE SCHEMA` on its schema and `USE CATALOG` on its catalog. Versions aren't securables of their own: the privileges on the model cover every version.

## Where each piece is stored

In the `uc-mlflow` environment, both services share one PostgreSQL server and one object store, but each keeps to its own database and its own bucket:

A gateway routes the Unity Catalog API to the server and the MLflow API to the tracking server, which serves its model registry from Unity Catalog. Both keep metadata in PostgreSQL (separate \`unitycatalog\` and \`mlflow\` databases) and files in RustFS (\`amzn-s3-demo-bucket\` and \`mlflow\` buckets).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    n0(["<b>Clients</b>"]):::clients
    n1{{"<b>Envoy</b><br/>gateway"}}:::gateway
    n2["<b>Postgres</b><br/>relational db"]:::component
    n3["<b>RustFS</b><br/>object store"]:::component
    n4["<b>Unity Catalog</b><br/>data catalog"]:::component
    n5["<b>MLflow</b><br/>experiment tracking"]:::component
    n0 -->|":8080"| n1
    n0 -->|":9000"| n1
    n1 -->|"/api/2.1/unity-catalog, /unity-catalog"| n4
    n1 -->|"/api/2.0/mlflow, /api/3.0/mlflow, /api/4.0/mlflow, /api/2.0/otel, /ai-gateway, /mlflow"| n5
    n1 -->|"S3 + STS"| n3
    n4 -->|"PostgreSQL: unitycatalog"| n2
    n4 -->|"S3: amzn-s3-demo-bucket"| n3
    n5 -->|"PostgreSQL: mlflow"| n2
    n5 -->|"S3: mlflow"| n3
    n5 -->|"HTTP"| n4
    classDef clients fill:#f1f5f9,stroke:#64748b
    classDef gateway fill:#ede9fe,stroke:#7c3aed
    classDef component fill:#eff6ff,stroke:#2563eb
    classDef external fill:#fafafa,stroke:#737373,stroke-dasharray: 4 3
```

| Object                                          | Owned by      | Metadata                | Files                                                    |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ------------- | ----------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| Experiment and run, with parameters and metrics | MLflow        | `mlflow` database       | —                                                        |
| Logged model, `models:/m-<id>`                  | MLflow        | `mlflow` database       | `mlflow` bucket, served by the tracking server           |
| Registered model                                | Unity Catalog | `unitycatalog` database | —                                                        |
| Model version                                   | Unity Catalog | `unitycatalog` database | `amzn-s3-demo-bucket` bucket, under the model's location |

Because each side keeps its own records and files, each survives the other's deletes. Deleting a model's versions and then the model in Unity Catalog leaves the run active, with its parameters and its logged model's files. Deleting the run, the logged model, and the logged model's files in MLflow leaves the version `READY`, and it still loads from Unity Catalog's storage.

## What registering a model version does

Registering a model version copies the logged model's files into a new version, in four steps that the MLflow client drives ([`create_model_version`](https://github.com/mlflow/mlflow/blob/v3.17.0/mlflow/store/_unity_catalog/registry/uc_oss_rest_store.py#L259-L297)):

1. **Create.** The client downloads the logged model's files from the tracking server and asks Unity Catalog to create the version, sending its `source` and `run_id`. The server assigns the version number and a storage location, and the version starts as `PENDING_REGISTRATION`.
2. **Get credentials.** The client asks Unity Catalog for temporary credentials with the `READ_WRITE_MODEL_VERSION` operation, scoped to that version's location ([`uc_oss_rest_store.py`](https://github.com/mlflow/mlflow/blob/v3.17.0/mlflow/store/_unity_catalog/registry/uc_oss_rest_store.py#L433-L456)). [Credential vending](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/credential-vending/) explains how the server mints them.
3. **Upload.** The client writes the files to the version's location with those credentials.
4. **Finalize.** The client tells Unity Catalog the upload is done, and the version becomes `READY`.

MLflow's client reaches Unity Catalog when its registry URI is `uc:<server URL>`, such as `uc:http://localhost:8080`. MLflow takes the server from the URI and a bearer token, if any, from the `MLFLOW_UC_OSS_TOKEN` environment variable ([`oss_registry_utils.py`](https://github.com/mlflow/mlflow/blob/v3.17.0/mlflow/utils/oss_registry_utils.py#L12-L29)). The tracking URI stays separate: the Unity Catalog store [has no tracking URI of its own](https://github.com/mlflow/mlflow/blob/v3.17.0/mlflow/store/_unity_catalog/registry/uc_oss_rest_store.py#L77-L79), so runs and logged models stay on the tracking server.

The logged model and its files stay in MLflow's store. Loading `models:/<catalog>.<schema>.<model>/<version>` reads the version's copy from Unity Catalog's storage, not from MLflow's.

## What the registry doesn't do

Unity Catalog's registry, and MLflow's store for it, leave out several features that other MLflow registries have:

- No aliases or stages. MLflow refuses to set aliases or move versions between stages, so `models:/<name>@<alias>` and `models:/<name>/latest` don't resolve. Load a version by its number instead.
- No tags. MLflow refuses to set tags on models and versions, and drops tags passed when registering without an error.
- No rename through MLflow. The Python SDK and the CLI rename a registered model.
- No serving. Registering deploys nothing, and loading runs the model in the loading process.

[Manage registered models](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/manage-models/) shows the error each of these raises.

| ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |

# https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/views-and-metric-views/

## Companion files

CI-tested scripts that run this page's examples end to end. A script that exits 0 has passed its checks.

They need Unity Catalog 0.7.0 running. To start it (also `environment` in this file's frontmatter):

```bash
curl -fsSL https://unitycatalog.io/docs/env/unitycatalog.tar.gz | tar -xz
cd uc-docs-env/unitycatalog && docker compose up -d --wait
export UNITY_CATALOG_URL=http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog
```

- [`stored_definitions.py`](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/views-and-metric-views/snippets/stored_definitions.py) (Python): What Unity Catalog stores for a SQL view and a metric view, and what it
  - run: `UNITY_CATALOG_URL=http://localhost:8080/api/2.1/unity-catalog uv run https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/views-and-metric-views/snippets/stored_definitions.py`

In [Unity Catalog](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/what-is-unity-catalog/ "The open-source reference server implementing the Unity Catalog specification."), a view is a catalog entry with a table type and a stored definition. It has no storage location and holds no data. When you query it, a query engine reads the definition from the catalog, expands it in its own dialect, and runs it against the source tables. A metric view is the same kind of entry, but its definition declares measures and dimensions in YAML instead of a query.

## What the catalog stores for a view

A view is stored as a table entry, so it's listed with the schema's tables and uses the same API. These fields set it apart:

| Field               | SQL view                              | Metric view                             |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| `table_type`        | `VIEW`                                | `METRIC_VIEW`                           |
| `view_definition`   | The query text after `AS`, as written | The YAML, as written                    |
| `columns`           | The output columns and their types    | The dimensions and measures, as columns |
| `view_dependencies` | The tables the query reads, if known  | The tables the YAML reads, at least one |
| `storage_location`  | Empty                                 | Empty                                   |

When it creates a view, the server checks the request's shape: there's a definition, at least one column, and every listed dependency exists ([`TableRepository`](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/blob/2b17f3b5a1d06c0adbf22f4c11ea888c01a36415/server/src/main/java/io/unitycatalog/server/persist/TableRepository.java#L972-L1000)). It stores the definition as sent. Spark sends the query text after `AS` with its line breaks and indentation.

> **Note**
>
> The server never parses a view's definition. A `VIEW` whose definition is the text `this is not a query` registers without error and is stored unchanged. The error comes later, from the engine that tries to run it.

When [Spark](https://spark.apache.org "Unified analytics engine for large-scale data processing.") creates a view, it also stores `properties` on the entry: the session's current catalog and namespace, the schema mode, the output column names, and the session's SQL settings, so it can read the view back the same way. Registering a view through the REST API generates none of these, so the entry holds only the properties the client sends. To register a view without Spark, see [Manage SQL views](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/sql-views/#register-a-view-through-the-rest-api).

## Where a view runs

The engine that reads a view runs it. It fetches the stored definition, parses it in its own SQL dialect, and plans the expanded query as if you had typed it. So a view's definition only works in engines that understand its dialect. A client that only talks to the REST API can store and return a definition, but it can't run one, and the Iceberg REST catalog serves no views.

For a SQL view, Spark works out the dependencies from the query as best it can. A view over `samples.views_explained.orders` records that table. A view with no source table, such as `SELECT 1 AS one`, records an empty list.

## SQL views versus metric views

Both kinds are stored definitions that an engine expands at query time. They differ in what the definition holds and how you query it:

|                  | SQL view                          | Metric view                                                             |
| ---------------- | --------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Definition       | A SQL query                       | YAML version `0.1`: a source, optional filter, dimensions, and measures |
| A query returns  | The query's rows                  | Measures aggregated over the dimensions you group by                    |
| How you query it | `SELECT` its columns like a table | `SELECT` dimensions, wrap each measure in `MEASURE()`, and `GROUP BY`   |
| Dependencies     | Optional                          | At least one, or the server rejects it                                  |

Use a SQL view to name a query: a join, a filter, or a renamed set of columns that several readers share. Use a metric view when the thing to share is a calculation, such as revenue or order count. Its readers then pick the grouping at query time, and every query computes the measure the same way. A metric view over the orders table with a `Revenue` measure of `SUM(amount)` returns revenue per status when you group by `Status`, and the grand total when you don't.

To work with each kind, see [Manage SQL views](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/sql-views/) and [Manage metric views](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/metric-views/).

## Changing a stored definition

The server checks a view once, when it's created. Dropping a source table later leaves the view listed, with `view_dependencies` still naming that table. Only a query against the view fails. The stored columns are checked only at read time too: they're a contract the engine plans against, and the server doesn't compare them with the query. Because the catalog can't update a view, a change means dropping it and creating it again, and the new entry gets the same checks. For the steps, see [Change or rename a view](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/sql-views/#change-or-rename-a-view) and [Change a metric view's definition](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/how-to/metric-views/#change-a-definition).

## Permissions

Because a view is a table entry, the server applies the table rules to it. These rules come from the server's source, linked at v0.7.0. The server has no row filters or column masks to attach to a view. For the privilege model itself, see [Ownership and privileges](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/uc-basics/#ownership-and-privileges).

- **Create a view:** the same privileges as creating a table. You need `USE CATALOG` on the catalog, or to own it, and you need either ownership of the schema or `USE SCHEMA` and `CREATE TABLE` on it ([`CREATE_TABLE`](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/blob/2b17f3b5a1d06c0adbf22f4c11ea888c01a36415/server/src/main/java/io/unitycatalog/server/auth/AuthorizeExpressions.java#L132-L141)).
- **Read a view's entry:** `USE CATALOG`, `USE SCHEMA`, and ownership, `SELECT`, or `MODIFY` on the view. The catalog's owner can read it too, and so can the schema's owner with `USE CATALOG` ([`GET_TABLE`](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/blob/2b17f3b5a1d06c0adbf22f4c11ea888c01a36415/server/src/main/java/io/unitycatalog/server/auth/AuthorizeExpressions.java#L30-L38), [`TableService`](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/blob/2b17f3b5a1d06c0adbf22f4c11ea888c01a36415/server/src/main/java/io/unitycatalog/server/service/TableService.java#L99-L117)). Listing a schema's tables returns only the views and tables you can read.

When a view is created, the server checks that its dependencies exist, not that the creator can read them ([`TableRepository`](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/blob/2b17f3b5a1d06c0adbf22f4c11ea888c01a36415/server/src/main/java/io/unitycatalog/server/persist/TableRepository.java#L972-L1000)). Reading the view's entry gives the engine the definition. Going by the server's source ([`TableService`](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/blob/2b17f3b5a1d06c0adbf22f4c11ea888c01a36415/server/src/main/java/io/unitycatalog/server/service/TableService.java#L99-L117)), the engine then reads each source table as the caller, so a view doesn't hide its source tables: a reader needs access to them as well.

- [Learn how ownership and privileges work](https://unitycatalog.io/docs/explanation/uc-basics/#ownership-and-privileges)
